L-space intervals for Graph Manifolds and CablesThanks: The author was supported by EPSRC grant EP/M000648/1

Sarah Dean Rasmussen Email address: S.Rasmussen@dpmms.cam.ac.uk Address: DPMMS
University of Cambridge
UK
Abstract.

We present a graph manifold analog of the Jankins-Neumann classification of Seifert fibered spaces over S2S^{2}\mkern-3.0mu admitting taut foliations, providing a finite recursive formula to compute the L-space Dehn-filling interval for any graph manifold with torus boundary. As an application of a generalization of this result to Floer simple manifolds, we compute the L-space interval for any cable of a Floer simple knot complement in a closed three-manifold in terms of the original L-space interval, recovering a result of Hedden and Hom as a special case.

Key words and phrases: 
graph manifold, taut foliation, L-space, Heegaard Floer

1. Introduction

In the late 1990’s, Thurston showed [36, 9] that any taut foliation on an atoroidal three-manifold MM makes π1​(M)\pi_{1}(M) act faithfully on the circle. This result came almost two decades after Eisenbud, Hirsch, and Neumann [12] encountered a complementary phenomenon: they proved that an oriented three-manifold MM Seifert fibered over S2S^{2} admits a co-oriented foliation transverse to the fiber if and only if π1​(M)\pi_{1}(M) admits a representation in Homeo+~​S1\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}S^{1} sending ϕ↦sh⁡(1)\phi\mkern-2.0mu\mapsto\mkern-2.0mu\mathrm{sh}(1), where Homeo+~​S1\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}S^{1} is the universal cover of the group of orientation-preserving homeomorphisms of the circle, ϕ\phi is the regular fiber class, and sh⁡(s):t↦t+s\mathrm{sh}(s)\mkern-1.5mu:\mkern-1.5mut\mapsto t\mkern-2.0mu+\mkern-2.0mus for any s∈ℝs\mkern-2.0mu\in\mkern-2.0mu{\mathbb{R}}, making Homeo+~​S1\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}\mkern-1.0muS^{1} the centralizer of sh⁡(1)\mathrm{sh}(1) in Homeo+​ℝ\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}{\mathbb{R}}.

1.1. Jankins-Neumann Classification

Inspired by this observation, Jankins and Neumann used Poincaré’s “rotation number” invariant to generalize the criterion of [12] to a more local representation-theoretic condition in terms of meridians of exceptional fibers. This new formulation of the problem, in addition to a correct conjecture that the necessary representation-theoretic conditions could be met in Homeo+~​S1\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}S^{1} if and only if they could also be met in a smooth Lie subgroup thereof, allowed them to work out a complete, explicit classification [23], which they proved in all but one special case, later proven by Naimi [28].

Theorem 1.1 ([23, 28]).

For n>1n>1, the manifold MS2​(y0,y1,…,yn)M_{S^{2}}(y_{0};y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}) Seifert fibered over S2S^{2} admits a co-oriented taut foliation if and only if 0=y−=y+\mkern 0.8mu0=y_{-}\mkern-2.5mu=y_{+}\mkern-2.5mu or 0∈⟨y+,y−⟩\mkern 0.8mu0\in\left<y_{+},y_{-}\right>, where

y−:=maxk>0−1k​(1+∑i=0n⌊yi​k⌋),y+:=mink>0−1k​(−1+∑i=0n⌈yi​k⌉).y_{-}:=\max_{k>0}-\mathord{\raise 0.49991pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.4pt}{}{1}{k}$}}\mkern-1.8mu\left(\mkern 2.0mu1+{{\textstyle{\sum\limits_{i=0}^{n}\left\lfloor y_{i}k\right\rfloor}}}\right),\;\;\;\;\;y_{+}:=\min_{k>0}-\mathord{\raise 0.49991pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.4pt}{}{1}{k}$}}\mkern-1.8mu\left(\mkern-3.0mu-1+{{\textstyle{\sum\limits_{i=0}^{n}\left\lceil y_{i}k\right\rceil}}}\right).

(In the above, and henceforth in this paper, we always regard kk as an integer, writing k>0k>0 as shorthand for the restriction k∈ℤ>0k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}.)

Since then, the Jankins-Neumann-Naimi classification has served as a Rosetta stone for certain a priori unrelated properties.

Theorem 1.2 ([12, 23, 28, 10, 30, 26, 27, 5, 33]).

If MM is a closed oriented Seifert fibered space, then the following are equivalent:

  1. (1a)

    π1​(M)\pi_{1}(M) admits a non-trivial representation in Homeo+​ℝ\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}{\mathbb{R}}.

  2. (1b)

    π1​(M)\pi_{1}(M) is left-orderable.

  3. (2)

    MM admits a co-oriented C0C^{\mkern 1.0mu0}\mkern-2.0mu taut foliation.

  4. (3)

    MM has non-trivial Heegaard Floer homology, i.e., MM fails to be an L-space.

One often uses (1​a)(1a) as a proxy for (1​b)(1b), since a result of Boyer, Wiest, and Rolfsen [6, Theorem 1.1.1], combined with the well-known fact [25] that the set of countable left-orderable groups coincides with the set of countable nontrivial subgroups of Homeo+​ℝ\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}{\mathbb{R}}, shows that (1​a)=(1​b)(1a)\!=\!(1b) for every prime compact oriented three-manifold. Boyer, Gordon, and Watson have conjectured that (1)=(3)(1)\!=\!(3) for any prime compact oriented three-manifold [5], and quite recently, Kazez and Roberts [24], and independently Bowden [3], have extended a C2C^{2} foliations result of Ozsváth and Szabó [30] to show that (2)⇒(3)(2)\!\Rightarrow\!(3) for any compact oriented three-manifold. (For this reason, all foliations in this paper are assumed to be C0C^{0} unless otherwise stated.)

The implication (3)⇒(2)(3)\!\Rightarrow\!(2), however, is entirely more mysterious. In particular, all known proofs [26, 27, 33] that non-L-space oriented Seifert fibered spaces admit co-oriented taut foliations rely on an explicit comparison of sets of manifolds: one works out the classification of Seifert fibered manifolds over S2S^{2}\! with non-trivial Heegaard Floer homology, and observes that this classification coincides with the Jankins-Neumann-Naimi classification of oriented Seifert fibered spaces over S2S^{2}\mkern-2.0mu admitting co-oriented taut foliations. (The implication (3)⇒\mkern-0.5mu(3)\mkern-3.5mu\Rightarrow\mkern-4.0mu (2)(2) holds vacuously for closed oriented Seifert fibered spaces with b1>0b_{1}\mkern-1.5mu>\mkern-1.5mu0, all of which admit co-oriented taut foliations [14], and for oriented Seifert fibered spaces over ℝ​ℙ2{\mathbb{R}}{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\!, all of which are L-spaces [5].)

1.2. Graph Manifolds

Boyer and Clay recently brought insight to this question by introducing a relative version of the problem, studying the gluing behavior of properties (1​a)(1a), (1​b)(1b), and (2)(2) along the incompressible tori separating Seifert fibered components of graph manifolds. By showing that these three properties glue in an identical manner along boundaries of JSJ components of rational homology sphere graph manifolds, they were able to prove the equivalence of these three properties for any closed graph manifold [4]. Boyer and Clay also conjectured that property (3)(3) should obey the same gluing behavior.

In answer, Hanselman and Watson [19], and independently J. Rasmussen and the author [33], were able to confirm this gluing conjecture for a larger class of three-manifolds with torus boundary, but subject to certain hypotheses, which one can show are safe to remove in the case of graph manifolds. The four of us [18] were therefore able to prove the following.

Theorem 1.3 ([18]).

A graph manifold is an L-space if and only if it fails to admit a co-oriented taut foliation.

The current paper follows an independent trajectory from the work of [18], launched before the author joined the other collaboration. Although the two papers overlap in one or two results, including slightly variant proofs of Theorem 1.3 and the below gluing criterion, the main result of the current paper is the generalization of the Jankins-Neumann classification formula to graph manifolds, for which we now introduce some notation.

Definition 1.4.

If YY\! is a compact oriented three-manifold with torus boundary, then the L-space interval of YY is the space ℒ⁡(Y)⊂ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y))\mathcal{L}(Y)\subset{\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)) of L-space Dehn filling slopes of YY\!.

We call ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y)\mkern-0.8mu an interval because if it contains more than one point, then it is the intersection of ℙ​(H1​(∂Y)){\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)) with either a closed interval in ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y,ℝ)){\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y;{\mathbb{R}})) or the complement of a single point in ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y,ℝ)){\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y;{\mathbb{R}})). It therefore makes sense to speak of the interior ℒ∘​(Y)\mathcal{L}^{\mkern-0.4mu\circ}\mkern-1.5mu(Y) of ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y). If ℒ∘​(Y)\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y) is nonempty, we call YY Floer simple.

Proposition 1.5.

If Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} are non-solid-torus graph manifolds with torus boundary, then the union Y1∪φY2Y_{1}\mkern-1.0mu\cup_{\varphi}\!Y_{2}, with gluing map φ:∂Y1→−∂Y2\varphi\mkern-1.0mu:\mkern-1.0mu\partial Y_{1}\to-\partial Y_{2}, is an L-space if and only if

φ∗ℙ​(ℒ∘​(Y1))∪ℒ∘​(Y2)=ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y2)).\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}\mkern-1.5mu(Y_{1}))\cup\mathcal{L}^{\circ}\mkern-1.5mu(Y_{2})={\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y_{2})).

In particular, Floer simplicity is not required.

A graph manifold YY with torus boundary and b1​(Y)>1b_{1}(Y)\mkern-1.5mu>\mkern-1.8mu1 has ℒ⁡(Y)=∅\mathcal{L}(Y)=\emptyset. Above, we see examples in which YY is Floer simple, has an isolated L-space filling, or has empty L-space interval. One cannot use Theorem 1.6 without first knowing which of these three cases occurs for YY. We therefore provide Proposition 4.7, which lists explicit criteria for the multiple mutually exclusive cases in which YY is Floer simple or in which YY has an isolated L-space filling. In the complement of these criteria, ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) is empty.

In fact, the validity of Theorem 4.6 extends beyond the realm of graph manifolds.

Proposition 1.7.

Theorem 1.6 holds for any boundary incompressible Floer simple three-manifolds Y1,…,YngY_{1},\ldots,Y_{n_{{\textsc{g}}}}, provided that YY satisfies the criteria in Proposition 4.7 for ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) to be nonempty.

One immediate application of this generalization is the computation of L-space intervals for cables of Floer simple knot complements.

1.3. Cables

The (p,q)(p,q)-cable Y(p,q)⊂XY^{(p,q)}\mkern-2.0mu\subset\mkern-2.0muX of a knot complement Y:=X∖ν⁡(K)⊂XY\mkern-2.0mu:=\mkern-2.0muX\mkern-1.5mu\setminus\mkern-1.5mu\nu(K)\subset X is given by the knot complement Y(p,q):=X∖ν⁡(K(p,q))Y^{(p,q)}\mkern-3.0mu:=\mkern-2.0muX\mkern-1.5mu\setminus\mkern-1.5mu\nu(K^{(p,q)}), where K(p,q)⊂XK^{(p,q)}\mkern-1.0mu\subset X is the image of the (p,q)(p,q)-torus knot embedded in the boundary of YY\!. Since one can realize any cable of Y⊂XY\subset X by gluing an appropriate Seifert fibered space onto YY\!, we can use the above generalization of Theorem 1.6 to prove the following result.

1.4. Generalized Solid Tori

A recent result of Gillespie [17] states that a compact oriented three manifold YY with torus boundary satisfies ℒ⁡(Y)=ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y))∖{l}\mathcal{L}(Y)={\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y))\setminus\{l\} if and only if YY has genus 0 and an L-space filling, where ll denotes the rational longitude of YY. Such manifolds are called generalized solid tori in [33] and are of independent interest [2, 15, 11, 1, 19].

Using the version of Theorem 1.8 that does not require XX to be an L-space, along with some incremental results from the proof of Theorem 1.6, we are able to show the following.

Theorem 1.10.

If YY is a generalized solid torus, then any cable of Y⊂Y⁡(l)Y\subset Y(l) is a generalized solid torus. If YY\! is a graph manifold with torus boundary, b1​(Y)=1b_{1}(Y)\mkern-2.5mu=\mkern-2.5mu1, and rational longitude other than the regular fiber, then YY is a generalized solid torus if and only if it is homeomorphic to an iterated cable of the regular fiber complement in S1×S2S^{1}\mkern-2.5mu\times\mkern-0.8muS^{2}\mkern-4.0mu.

Similarly, for any class of manifolds for which the gluing result in Proposition 1.5 holds without the requirement of Floer simplicity—such as graph manifolds—one has the result that if YY has an isolated L-space filling, i.e., if ℒ⁡(Y)={μ}\mathcal{L}(Y)=\{\mu\} for some μ∈ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y))\mu\in{\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)), then any cable of Y⊂Y⁡(μ)Y\subset Y(\mu) has Y⁡(μ)Y(\mu) as an isolated L-space filling.

1.5. Floer simple knot complements

Whereas the regular fiber complement in a rational homology sphere Seifert fibered space could arguably be called the prototypical Floer simple manifold, not every regular fiber complement in an L-space graph manifold is Floer simple, due to the existence of isolated L-space fillings. However, the next best thing is true.

Given a closed graph manifold XX, call an exceptional fiber fe⊂Xf_{\textsc{e}}\mkern-1.5mu\subset\mkern-2.5muX invariantly exceptional if the JSJ component Y^⊂X\hat{Y}\subset X containing fef_{\textsc{e}} has more than one exceptional fiber. Note that if Y^\hat{Y} has only one exceptional fiber, then Y^\hat{Y} is either a lens space (if XX is Seifert fibered) or a punctured solid torus. Since the solid torus has nonunique Seifert structure, one can show that if XX is not a lens space, it is homeomorphic to a graph manifold X′X^{\prime} in which the image fe′f_{\textsc{e}}^{\prime} of fef_{\textsc{e}} is a regular fiber. excluding this scenario allows us to show the following.

Theorem 1.11.

Every invariantly exceptional fiber complement in an L-space graph manifold is Floer simple.

There are also Floer simple knot complements traversing the graph structure of XX.

Proposition 1.12.

If XX is an L-space graph manifold, then for every incompressible torus T⊂XT\subset X, there is a knot K⊂XK\subset X transversely intersecting TT for which the complement X∖ν⁡(K)X\setminus\nu(K) is Floer simple.

The same occurs for an arbitrary L-space XX, provided that XX decomposes as a union of Floer simple manifolds along TT (see Proposition 6.6).

The above results, together with the evidence of various other classes of L-spaces, and a certain degree of optimism, motivate the following:

Conjecture 1.13.

Every L-space admits a Floer simple knot complement.

1.6. Organization

In Section 2, we introduce our conventions for Seifert fibered spaces and provide a lengthy discussion of the Jankins-Neumann problem, since we cannot hope for Theorem 1.6 to provide insight if the original theorem of Jankins, Neumann and Naimi is opaque to the reader.

Section 3 reviews some basic facts about L-space intervals, including the independent results of Hanselman and Watson [19] and J. Rasmussen and the author [33] about L-space criteria for unions of Floer simple manifolds.

Section 4 is where we prove our main graph manifold results, including Theorems 1.3 and 1.6 in the forms of Theorems 4.5 and 4.6. This section also derives Proposition 4.7’s classification of single-boundary-component graph manifolds with nonempty L-space intervals.

Our main cabling results reside in Section 5, although the proof of Theorem 1.10, for generalized solid tori, is relegated to Section 6.

Lastly, Section 6 justifies Proposition 1.7’s generalization of our Jankins-Neumann graph manifold result to the union of a Seifert fibered space with Floer simple manifolds. This final section also lists an array of applications of the paper’s main results, including the aforementioned generalized solid torus cabling result and proofs of the Floer simple knot complement results from Theorem 1.11 and Proposition 1.12.

2. Foliations on Seifert fibered spaces

A graph manifold is a prime compact oriented three-manifold which admits a JSJ decomposition—which in this case, we take to be a minimal cutting apart along incompressible tori into disjoint pieces—such that each JSJ component is an oriented Seifert fibered space. The data for reassembling these components into the original manifold are encoded in a labeled graph, where each vertex corresponds to a Seifert fibered JSJ component, and each edge corresponds to a gluing of two Seifert fibered pieces along an incompressible torus.

2.1. Restricting taut foliations to JSJ components

Questions about taut foliations on graph manifolds can often be reduced to questions about taut foliations on Seifert fibered spaces, due in part to the following result.

Proposition 2.1 ([34, 35, 8]).

If YY is a compact oriented three-manifold admitting a taut foliation FF transverse to ∂Y\partial Y, then every incompressible separating torus in YY can be isotoped to be everywhere transverse to FF.

Proof.

Roussarie [34] showed that if FF is C2C^{2}, then each incompressible torus T⊂YT\subset Y can be isotoped to be either everywhere transverse to FF or a leaf of FF. A later theorem of Brittenham and Roberts [8] extends the validity of this proposition to C0C^{0} foliations. Thus, since a taut foliation has no compact separating leaves, an incompressible separating torus cannot be isotoped to be a leaf of FF, and so it must be possible to isotop any incompressible separating torus to be everywhere transverse to FF. This is also believed to have been known by Thurston [35]. ∎

As noted by Brittenham, Naimi, and Roberts [7], this result has major consequences for graph manifolds:

Corollary 2.2.

If YY\! is a graph manifold with tree graph and FF is a taut foliation on YY transverse to ∂Y\partial Y, then FF can be isotoped so that it restricts to boundary-transverse taut foliations on the Seifert fibered JSJ components of YY.

When a closed graph manifold has positive first Betti number, the question of existence of taut foliations becomes trivial, since a result of Gabai states that any such manifold admits a co-oriented taut foliation [14]. Correspondingly, any closed oriented three manifold with b1>0b_{1}\!>\!0 has non-trivial Heegaard Floer homology, hence is not an L-space. We therefore restrict attention to rational homology sphere graph manifolds, hence to oriented Seifert fibered spaces over S2S^{2}\mkern-1.0mu or ℝ​ℙ2\mkern 0.5mu{\mathbb{R}}{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\!, and regular fiber complements thereof.

Remark. The requirement that risi≠∞\frac{r_{i}}{s_{i}}\neq\infty for i∈{0,…,n}i\in\{0,\ldots,n\} is a necessary (assuming n>1n\mkern-2.0mu>\mkern-2.0mu1) and sufficient condition for the resulting Seifert fibered space to be prime—an important property for manifolds serving as building blocks in combinatorial constructions. To understand necessity, let M^∞\hat{M}^{\infty} denote the result of Dehn filling M^\hat{M} with slope ∞\infty along ∂0M^\partial_{0}\hat{M}. If M^\hat{M} is fibered over a punctured S2S^{2}, then M^∞\hat{M}^{\infty} is a connected sum of nn solid tori, each with longitude of slope ∞\infty. Similarly, if M^\hat{M} is fibered over a punctured ℝ​ℙ2{\mathbb{R}}{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, then M^∞\hat{M}^{\infty} is the connected sum of an S1×S2S^{1}\mkern-2.0mu\times\mkern-1.0muS^{2} with nn solid tori, each with longitude of slope ∞\infty.

Primality is especially important in the context of foliations, since, by Novikov [29], no reducible manifold except S1×S2S^{1}\mkern-2.0mu\times\mkern-1.0muS^{2} admits a co-oriented taut foliation. On the other hand, not all connected sums are L-spaces, so any correspondence between being an L-space and failing to admit a co-oriented taut foliation breaks down beyond the realm of prime manifolds.

2.3. Rotation Number, Shift, and Foliation Slope

One of the key insights of Jankins and Neumann into the work of Eisenbud, Hirsch, and Neumann on taut foliations on Seifert fibered spaces was the need for a better invariant on Homeo+~​S1\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}S^{1}​. Whereas the latter group relied on the invariants m¯,m¯:Homeo+~​S1→ℝ\underline{m},\overline{m}:\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}S^{1}\to{\mathbb{R}}, with m¯​(γ):=mint∈ℝ⁡γ⁡(t)−t\underline{m}(\gamma):=\min_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\gamma(t)-t and m¯​(γ):=maxt∈ℝ⁡γ⁡(t)−t\overline{m}(\gamma):=\max_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\gamma(t)-t, Jankins and Neumann introduced the problem to a more precise invariant of circle actions: a conjugacy invariant called the (Poincaré) rotation number,

(9) rot:Homeo+~​(S1)→ℝ,rot⁡(γ)=limk→∞1k​(γk​(t)−t),\mathrm{rot}:\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}(S^{1})\to{\mathbb{R}},\;\;\;\mathrm{rot}(\gamma)=\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathord{\raise 0.49991pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.4pt}{}{1}{k}$}}(\gamma^{k}(t)-t),

which is independent of t∈ℝt\in{\mathbb{R}}, and rational if and only if γ\gamma has some closed orbit [16]. The rotation number is not, in general, a homomorphism. However, it restricts to a homomorphism on any amenable, hence any abelian, subgroup [16]. In particular, it restricts to a homomorphism on any representation of the fundamental group of a torus.

The simplest element of Homeo+~​(S1)\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}(S^{1}) is a rotation, or shift,

(10) sh⁡(s):t↦t+s,t∈ℝ.\mathrm{sh}(s):t\mapsto t+s,\;\;\;t\in{\mathbb{R}}.

Whereas rot∘sh=id\mathrm{rot}\circ\mkern 0.4mu\mathrm{sh}\mkern-1.0mu=\mkern-1.0mu\mathrm{id}, not every element of Homeo+~​(S1)\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}(S^{1}) is conjugate to a rotation. It is a classic result, however, that every element of Homeo+~​(S1)\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}(S^{1}) with irrational rotation number is left and right semiconjugate to a shift of the same rotation number [16].

Rotation numbers can also be used to associate slopes to taut foliations on tori.

Definition 2.4.

For the two-torus TT, there is a canonical map

(11) α:{C0​ codimension-one foliations on ​T}→ℙ⁡(H1​(T,ℝ)),\alpha:\left\{\;C^{0}\mkern-2.0mu\text{ codimension-one foliations on }T\;\right\}\;\to\;{\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(T;{\mathbb{R}})),

constructed below, which respects isotopy. We call α⁡(F)\alpha(F) the slope of FF.

If FF has Reeb compenents, then α⁡(F)\alpha(F) is given by the class of any closed leaf of FF. All Reebless foliations on tori are taut. Thus, if FF is Reebless, then there is a curve, say CλC_{\lambda} of primitive class λ∈H1​(T)\lambda\in H_{1}(T), which intersects every leaf transversely, and FF can be realized as the suspension of a circle homeomorphism γF,λ∈Homeo+​S1\gamma_{F,\lambda}\in\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}S^{1} from CλC_{\lambda} to itself [20]. A choice of μ∈H1​(T)\mu\in H_{1}(T) with μ⋅λ=1\mu\cdot\lambda=1 induces a lift of this suspension to a suspension from a universal cover C~λ\tilde{C}_{\lambda} of CλC_{\lambda} to its translate by μ\mu in the universal cover of TT. That is, if we regard C~λ\tilde{C}_{\lambda} as the real vector space {t​λ}t∈ℝ\{t\lambda\}_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}} spanned by λ\lambda, with Cλ≅C~λ/λ​ℤC_{\lambda}\cong\tilde{C}_{\lambda}/\lambda{\mathbb{Z}}, then one can lift the foliation FF to the universal cover of TT by iteratively suspending the map t​λ↦γ~F,λ,μ​(t)​λ+μt\lambda\mapsto\tilde{\gamma}_{\mkern 0.2muF,\lambda,\mu}(t)\lambda+\mu, for an appropriate lift γ~F,λ,μ∈Homeo~+​S1⊂Homeo+​ℝ\tilde{\gamma}_{F,\lambda,\mu}\in\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}}_{+}S^{1}\subset\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}{\mathbb{R}}\mkern 0.8mu of γF,λ∈Homeo+​S1\mkern 0.5mu\gamma_{F,\lambda}\in{\mathrm{Homeo}}_{+}S^{1}.

This lifted suspsension, in turn, induces a representation

(12) ρλF:π1​(T)→Homeo~+​S1,[λ]↦sh⁡(1),[−μ]↦γ~F,λ,μ,\rho^{F}_{\lambda}:\pi_{1}(T)\to\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}}_{+}S^{1},\;\;\;\;[\lambda]\mapsto\mathrm{sh}(1),\;\;\;\;[-\mu]\mapsto\tilde{\gamma}_{F,\lambda,\mu},

where [λ][\lambda] and [μ][\mu] denote the lifts of λ\lambda and μ\mu to π1​(T)\pi_{1}(T). One can regard ρλF\rho^{F}_{\lambda} as describing how to traverse the line {t​λ}t∈ℝ⊂⟨μ,λ⟩ℝ\{t\lambda\}_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\subset\left<\mu,\lambda\right>_{{\mathbb{R}}} by traveling only along foliation leaves or integer multiples of λ\lambda or μ\mu. That is, if one starts at some t0​λt_{0}\lambda, hops by a​λ+b​μa\lambda+b\mu for some a,b∈ℤa,b\in{\mathbb{Z}}, takes the foliation leaf intersecting this new point, and follows this leaf back to the line {t​λ}t∈ℝ\{t\lambda\}_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}, then one will arrive at ρλF​(a​λ+b​μ)​(t0)​λ\rho^{F}_{\lambda}(a\lambda+b\mu)(t_{0})\lambda. Note that while ρλF\rho^{F}_{\lambda} is independent of the choice of μ\mu, and is determined up to conjugacy by a choice of λ\lambda, it still depends on λ\lambda.

On the other hand, when we define the slope α⁡(F)\alpha(F) of FF to be

(13) α(F):=ker(rot∘ρλF)=⟨(rot(ρλF(−μ))λ+μ⟩∈ℙ(H1(T;ℝ)),\alpha(F):={{\text{ker}\ }}(\mathrm{rot}\circ\rho^{F}_{\lambda})=\left<(\mathrm{rot}(\rho^{F}_{\lambda}\!(-\mu))\lambda+\mu\right>\in{\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(T;{\mathbb{R}})),

then the rotation number washes out all dependence on λ\lambda and choice of suspension. That is, one can use the definition of rotation number to compute rot⁡(ρλF​(−μ))\mathrm{rot}(\rho^{F}_{\lambda}\!(-\mu)) in terms of the rotation number associated to a different choice of basis and suspension for FF, and obtain the same answer for α⁡(F)\alpha(F) in both cases. Alternatively, any suspension homeomorphism with rational rotation number has a periodic orbit, hence realizes a foliation with a compact leaf of slope α⁡(F)\alpha(F). If the suspension homeomorphism has irrational rotation number, then it is semiconjugate to a shift of matching rotation number [16], giving rise to a linear foliation of slope α⁡(F)\alpha(F).

2.4. Restricting Seifert fibered space foliations to torus foliations

If a compact oriented three-manifold YY admits a co-oriented taut foliation transverse to ∂Y\partial Y, then Gabai tells us that ∂Y\partial Y can only have toroidal components [14]. Thus, we often encounter foliations on tori as boundary restrictions of foliations on three-manifolds. Moreover, on a Seifert fibered space, any taut foliation transverse to the boundary restricts to taut foliations on boundary components.

Suppose FF is a co-oriented taut foliation transverse to the fibration of the Seifert fibered Dehn filling MS2​(r∗s∗)M_{S^{2}\mkern-2.0mu}(\frac{r_{*}}{s_{*}}) along the slopes r∗s∗=(r0s0,…,rnsn)\frac{r_{*}}{s_{*}}=(\frac{r_{0}}{s_{0}},\ldots,\frac{r_{n}}{s_{n}}) of the trivial circle fibration M^\hat{M} over an n+1n\!+\!1-punctured S2S^{2}, according to the conventions of Section 2.2. For each boundary component ∂iM^\partial_{i}\hat{M}, we regard the foliation F∩∂iM^F\cap\partial_{i}\hat{M} as a suspension of a homemorphism of the curve of class f~i\tilde{f}_{i} to itself, and since the class −h~i-\tilde{h}_{i} satisfies −h~i⋅f~i=1-\tilde{h}_{i}\cdot\tilde{f}_{i}=1, it specifies a lift of this suspension to a suspension of an element γF,f~i,−h~i∈Homeo+~​S1\gamma_{F,\tilde{f}_{i},-\tilde{h}_{i}}\in\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}S^{1}. To this suspension we associate the representation

(14) ρi:=ρf~iF∩∂iM^:π1​(∂iM^)→Homeo+~​S1,[f~i]→sh⁡(1),[h~i]→γF,f~i,−h~i,\rho_{i}:=\rho^{F\mkern 0.3mu\cap\mkern 0.3mu\partial_{i}\mkern-1.2mu\hat{M}}_{\mkern-2.3mu\tilde{f}_{i}}:\pi_{1}(\partial_{i}\hat{M})\to\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}S^{1}\mkern-2.0mu,\;\;\;\;[\tilde{f}_{i}]\to\mathrm{sh}(1),\;\;\;\;[\tilde{h}_{i}]\to\gamma_{F,\tilde{f}_{i},-\tilde{h}_{i}},

allowing us to express the slope α⁡(F∩∂iM^)\alpha(F\cap\partial_{i}\hat{M}) of F∩∂iM^F\cap\partial_{i}\hat{M} as

(15) α⁡(F∩∂iM^)=πi​(rot⁡(ρi​([h~i]))​f~i−h~i)=rot⁡(ρi​([h~i])).\alpha(F\cap\partial_{i}\hat{M})=\pi_{i}(\mathrm{rot}(\rho_{i}([\tilde{h}_{i}]))\tilde{f}_{i}-\tilde{h}_{i})=\mathrm{rot}(\rho_{i}([\tilde{h}_{i}])).

The construction of Eisenbud, Hirsch, and Neumann [12] associating a representation ρ:π1​(M⁡(risi))→Homeo+~​S1\rho:\pi_{1}(M(\frac{r_{i}}{s_{i}}))\to\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}S^{1} to FF, sending the fiber class ϕ=[f]\phi=[f] to sh⁡(1)\mathrm{sh}(1), is sufficiently compatible with the construction of each ρi\rho_{i} above that, possibly after conjugation of each ρi\rho_{i}, ρ\rho can be chosen to satisfy ρi=ρ∘ιiπ1\rho_{i}=\rho\circ\iota^{\pi_{1}}_{i}, with ιiπ1:π1​(∂iM^)→π1​(MS2​(r∗s∗))\iota^{\pi_{1}}_{i}:\pi_{1}(\partial_{i}\hat{M})\to\pi_{1}(M_{S^{2}\mkern-2.0mu}(\frac{r_{*}}{s_{*}})) the homomorphism induced by inclusion. The presentation (6) for π1​(MS2​(r∗s∗))\pi_{1}(M_{S^{2}}(\frac{r_{*}}{s_{*}})) then places the following restrictions on ρ\rho, as observed by Jankins and Neumann [23]:

Jankins and Neumann mostly focused on the case of n=3n=3, e0=−1e_{0}=-1, and 0<r1s1,r2s2,r3s3<10<\frac{r_{1}}{s_{1}},\frac{r_{2}}{s_{2}},\frac{r_{3}}{s_{3}}<1, but their above observation holds in general.

Whereas the first condition enforces a global restriction on FF, the latter two conditions provide local restrictions at each F∩∂iM^F\cap\partial_{i}\hat{M}, which we could recover simply by considering Dehn fillings. The solid torus admits only one taut foliation, namely, the product foliation with slope given by the rational longitude. As a consequence, the co-oriented taut foliation F∩∂iM^F\cap\partial_{i}\hat{M} extends to a co-oriented taut foliation on the Dehn filling ∂iM^​(risi)\partial_{i}\hat{M}(\frac{r_{i}}{s_{i}}) if and only if F∩∂iM^F\cap\partial_{i}\hat{M} is the product foliation of slope risi\frac{r_{i}}{s_{i}}, which occurs if and only if ρi​([h~i])=ρ⁡(ηi)\rho_{i}([\tilde{h}_{i}])\!=\!\rho(\eta_{i}) is conjugate to sh⁡(risi)\mathrm{sh}(\frac{r_{i}}{s_{i}}), a condition which requires α⁡(F∩∂iM^)=rot⁡(ρ⁡(ηi))=risi\alpha(F\cap\partial_{i}\hat{M})=\mathrm{rot}(\rho(\eta_{i}))=\frac{r_{i}}{s_{i}}. In particular, the jthj^{\mathrm{th}} shift conjugacy condition, that ρ⁡(ηj)\rho(\eta_{j}) be conjugate to sh⁡(rjsj)\mathrm{sh}(\frac{r_{j}}{s_{j}}), is due solely to the fact that ∂jM^\partial_{j}\hat{M} is glued to a solid torus. As emphasized by Boyer and Clay [4], when one relaxes the jthj^{\mathrm{th}} shift conjugacy condition, one can still find manifolds YY with torus boundary for which FF extends to a taut foliation on M^∪∂jM^Y\hat{M}\cup_{\partial_{j}\mkern-1.5mu\hat{M}}\mkern-2.0muY\!, for a suitable choice of gluing map.

It is presumably for this reason that Jankins and Neumann focused on the more general condition of JJ-realizability for an n+1n\!+\!1-tuple r∗s∗:=(e0=r0s0,r1s1,…,rnsn)\frac{r_{*}}{s_{*}}\mkern-2.0mu:=\mkern-2.0mu(e_{0}\mkern-4.0mu=\mkern-4.0mu\frac{r_{0}}{s_{0}},\frac{r_{1}}{s_{1}},\ldots,\frac{r_{n}}{s_{n}}), given a subset J⊂{1,…,n}J\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}. They deem r∗s∗\frac{r_{*}}{s_{*}} JJ-realizable if there is a representation ρJ:⟨η1,…​ηn⟩→Homeo+~​S1\rho^{J}:\left<\eta_{1},\ldots\eta_{n}\right>\to\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}S^{1} such that ρJ\rho^{J} meets the r∗s∗\frac{r_{*}}{s_{*}} rotation number condition, that rot⁡(∏i=1nρ⁡(ηi))=−e0\mathrm{rot}\mkern-2.0mu\left({\textstyle{\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mkern-3.5mu\rho(\eta_{i})\mkern-1.3mu}}\right)\mkern-2.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu-e_{0} with rot⁡(ρ⁡(ηi))=risi\mathrm{rot}(\rho(\eta_{i}))\!=\!\textstyle{\frac{r_{i}}{s_{i}}} for each i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, and such that ρJ\rho^{J} meets the jthj^{\mathrm{th}} shift conjugacy condition for each j∈Jj\in J. We have already shown that JJ-realizability is a necessary condition for M^\hat{M} to admit a taut foliation FF of slopes α⁡(F∩∂iM^)=risi\alpha(F\cap\partial_{i}\hat{M})=\frac{r_{i}}{s_{i}} which extends to a taut foliation on the partial Dehn filling of M^\hat{M} along the slopes rjsj∈ℙ⁡(H1​(∂jM^))\frac{r_{j}}{s_{j}}\in{\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial_{j}\hat{M})) for all j∈{0}∪Jj\in\{0\}\cup J. With the help of Naimi, Jankins and Neumann showed that the condition is also sufficient [23, 28].

2.6. Dehn fillings and N¯\bar{N}-fillings

For any particular i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\} in the above theorem, if one fixes the remaining slopes, one finds that the space of slopes in ℙ⁡(H1​(∂iM^)){\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial_{i}\hat{M})) for which the desired taut foliation exists is often an interval. We now introduce some notation to describe such spaces of slopes in general.

Definition 2.6.

If Y\mkern 0.5muY\mkern-3.8mu is a compact oriented three-manifold with torus boundary, then we define the sets ℱL​(Y)⊂ℱD​(Y)⊂ℱ⁡(Y)⊂ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y,ℤ))\mathcal{F}^{L}\mkern-1.6mu(Y)\mkern-3.0mu\subset\mkern-2.4mu\mathcal{F}^{D}\mkern-2.2mu(Y)\mkern-3.0mu\subset\mkern-2.4mu\mathcal{F}\mkern-0.5mu(Y)\mkern-3.0mu\subset\mkern-2.0mu{\mathbb{P}}(H_{\mkern-0.2mu1}\mkern-0.5mu(\partial Y\mkern-0.6mu;{\mathbb{Z}})\mkern-1.5mu)\mkern-1.8mu of rational foliation slopes as follows:

ℱL​(Y)\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{L}\mkern-2.0mu(Y) :={α(F∩∂Y)|F​ is a co-oriented taut foliation on ​Y​ transverse to ​∂Y,restricting to a rational co-oriented linear foliation on ​∂Y},\displaystyle:=\left\{\alpha(F\cap\partial Y)\left|\mkern-4.0mu\begin{array}[]{c}F\text{ is a co-oriented taut foliation on }Y\!\text{ transverse to }\partial Y,\\ \text{restricting to a rational co-oriented {{linear}} foliation on }\partial Y\end{array}\mkern-10.0mu\right.\right\},
ℱD​(Y)\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{D}\mkern-2.0mu(Y) :={μ|The Dehn filling Y(μ) admits a co-oriented taut foliation},\displaystyle:=\left\{\mkern 39.2mu\mu\mkern 39.2mu\left|\mkern 7.0mu\text{The Dehn filling }Y\mkern-1.2mu(\mu)\text{ admits a co-oriented taut foliation}\mkern 5.0mu\right.\right\},
ℱ⁡(Y)\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(Y) :={α(F∩∂Y)|F is a co-oriented taut foliation on Y transverse to ∂Y}.\displaystyle:=\left\{\mkern 3.5mu\alpha(F\cap\partial Y)\mkern 1.5mu\left|\mkern 15.0muF\text{ is a co-oriented taut foliation on }Y\!\text{ transverse to }\partial Y\mkern 6.0mu\right.\right\}.

All linear foliations, even irrational ones, are taut, but rational linear foliations are product foliations, hence extend to co-oriented taut foliations on Dehn fillings of matching slope, implying ℱL​(Y)⊂ℱD​(Y)⊂ℱ⁡(Y)\mathcal{F}^{L}(Y)\mkern-2.0mu\subset\mkern-2.0mu\mathcal{F}^{D}(Y)\mkern-2.0mu\subset\mkern-2.0mu\mathcal{F}(Y). In fact, the work of Jankins and Neumann tells us that ℱL=ℱD\mathcal{F}^{L}\mkern-3.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu\mathcal{F}^{D} for manifolds Seifert fibered over the disk, and that the analogous result holds for manifolds Seifert fibered over a punctured S2S^{2}. Since the same also holds for manifolds Seifert fibered over a punctured ℝ​ℙ2{\mathbb{R}}{\mathbb{P}}^{2} [4], and since Corollary 2.2 tells us that taut foliations on homology sphere graph manifolds isotop to restrict to taut foliations transverse to boundaries on Seifert fibered JSJ components, we additionally have ℱL=ℱD\mathcal{F}^{L}\mkern-3.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu\mathcal{F}^{D} for any graph manifold with torus boundary and b1=1b_{1}=1.

In this latter case, it is natural to ask whether ℱ⁡(Y)\mathcal{F}(Y) admits a description analogous to the Dehn filling characterization for ℱL​(Y)\mathcal{F}^{L}\mkern-1.2mu(Y). That is, can ℱ⁡(Y)\mathcal{F}(Y) be characterized in terms of taut foliations on some closed union of YY with some other manifold? Boyer and Clay answer this question affirmatively [4], as we shall see.

Let N¯\bar{N} denote the regular fiber complement

(24) N¯:=MS2​(0,−12,12)∖(S1×D02),\bar{N}:=M_{S^{2}}(0,{\textstyle{-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}}})\setminus(S^{1}\!\times\!D^{2}_{0}),

which Boyer and Clay call the “twisted II-bundle over the Klein bottle,” or N2N_{2}. The manifold N¯\bar{N} can play a role analogous to that of the solid torus for Dehn fillings.

Definition 2.7.

Suppose YY is an oriented three-manifold with toroidal boundary component ∂iY\partial_{i}Y. We call any union Y∪φN¯Y\cup_{\varphi}\mkern-3.0mu\bar{N} with gluing map φ:∂N¯→−∂iY\varphi:\partial\bar{N}\to-\partial_{i}Y an N¯\bar{N}-filling of YY\! along μ∈ℙ⁡(H1​(∂iY))\mu\in{\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial_{i}Y)), where μ:=φ∗ℙ​(l)\mu:=\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(l) is the image of the rational longitude ll of N¯\bar{N}. If YY has (single) torus boundary, we denote an N¯\bar{N}-filling of YY along μ∈ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y))\mu\in{\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)) by YN¯​(μ)Y^{\mkern-1.0mu\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\mu).

More generally, if ∂Y=∐i=1n∂iY\partial Y=\coprod_{i=1}^{n}\partial_{i}Y is a disjoint union of tori, then given a slope μ∗:=(μ1,…,μn)∈∏i=1nℙ⁡(H1​(∂iY))\mu_{*}\mkern-2.5mu:\mkern-0.4mu=\mkern-2.0mu(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n})\mkern-2.0mu\in\mkern-2.0mu\prod_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial_{i}Y)) and subset J¯⊂{1,…,n}\bar{J}\subset\{1,\dots,n\}, we denote by YN¯​(J¯,μ∗)Y^{\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\bar{J};\mu_{*}) any manifold resulting from N¯\bar{N}-filling YY\! along μȷ¯\mu_{\bar{\jmath}} in ∂ȷ¯Y\partial_{\bar{\jmath}}Y\mkern-2.5mu for each ȷ¯∈J¯\bar{\jmath}\in\bar{J}.

We then have the following result for N¯\bar{N}-fillings.

Proposition 2.8.

Suppose YY\! is a prime compact oriented manifold with boundary a disjoint union ∐i=1n∂iY\coprod_{i=1}^{n}\partial_{i}Y\! of tori, with some given slope μ∗:=(μ1,…,μn)∈∏i=1nℙ⁡(H1​(∂iY))\mu_{*}\mkern-2.5mu:\mkern-0.4mu=\mkern-2.0mu(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n})\mkern-2.0mu\in\mkern-2.0mu\prod_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial_{i}Y)). Moreover, suppose either that b1​(Y⁡(μ∗))>0b_{1}(Y(\mu_{*}))>0 for the Dehn filling Y⁡(μ∗)Y(\mu_{*}), or that YY\! is a graph manifold, and there is some (possibly empty) J¯⊂{1,…,n}\bar{J}\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}, and N¯\bar{N}-filling YN¯​(J¯,μ∗)Y^{\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\bar{J};\mu_{*}) of YY\! along μȷ¯\mu_{\bar{\jmath}} in ∂ȷ¯Y\partial_{\bar{\jmath}}Y\mkern-2.5mu for each ȷ¯∈J¯\bar{\jmath}\in\bar{J}, such that YN¯​(J¯,μ∗)Y^{\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\bar{J};\mu_{*}) admits a co-oriented taut foliation FF transverse to the boundary, with α⁡(F∩∂jY)=μj\alpha(F\cap\partial_{j}Y)\mkern-1.5mu=\mkern-1.5mu\mu_{j} for each j∈J:={1,…,n}∖J¯j\mkern-2.0mu\in\mkern-2.0muJ\mkern-2.0mu:\mkern-0.3mu=\mkern-2.0mu\{1,\ldots,n\}\mkern-2.0mu\setminus\mkern-2.0mu\bar{J}.

Then, for every J¯⊂{1,…,n}\bar{J}\mkern-2.0mu\subset\mkern-2.0mu\{1,\ldots,n\}, every N¯\bar{N}-filling YN¯​(J¯,μ∗)Y^{\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\bar{J};\mu_{*}) (including Y:=YN¯​(∅,μ∗)Y\mkern-2.0mu:\mkern-0.3mu=\mkern-2.0muY^{\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\emptyset;\mu_{*})) admits a co-oriented taut foliation FF transverse to the boundary, with α⁡(F∩∂jY)=μj\alpha(F\cap\partial_{j}Y)\mkern-1.5mu=\mkern-1.5mu\mu_{j} for each j∈J:={1,…,n}∖J¯j\mkern-2.0mu\in\mkern-2.0muJ\mkern-2.0mu:\mkern-0.3mu=\mkern-2.0mu\{1,\ldots,n\}\mkern-2.0mu\setminus\mkern-2.0mu\bar{J}.

Proof.

Part (2) of Gabai’s main theorem in [14] tells us that any prime oriented three-manifold with b1>0b_{1}\mkern-2.0mu>\mkern-2.0mu0 and boundary a (possibly empty) union of tori admits a co-oriented taut foliation transverse to the boundary. Thus, if b1​(Y⁡(μ∗))>0b_{1}(Y(\mu_{*}))\mkern-2.0mu>\mkern-2.0mu0, then any N¯\bar{N}-filling YN¯​(μ∗):=YN¯​({1,…,n},μ∗)Y^{\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\mu_{*})\mkern-1.5mu:=\mkern-1.5muY^{\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\{1,\ldots,n\};\mu_{*}) has b1>0b_{1}>0, hence admits a co-oriented taut foliation FF. Since each ∂iY\partial_{i}Y is an incompressible separating torus in this N¯\bar{N}-filling, Proposition 2.1 allows us to isotop these separating tori so that they are everywhere transverse to FF. Restricting FF to any sub-N¯\bar{N}-filling YN¯​(J¯,μ∗)⊂YN¯​(μ∗)Y^{\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\bar{J};\mu_{*})\subset Y^{\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\mu_{*}) then gives the desired taut foliation on YN¯​(J¯,μ∗)Y^{\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\bar{J};\mu_{*}).

If instead, YY is a graph manifold with b1​(Y⁡(μ∗))=0b_{1}(Y(\mu_{*}))=0, and we are given J¯⊂{1,…,n}\bar{J}\mkern-2.0mu\subset\mkern-2.0mu\{1,\ldots,n\} and a co-oriented taut foliation FF on some N¯\bar{N}-filling YN¯​(J¯,μ∗)Y^{\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\bar{J};\mu_{*}), with FF transverse to the boundary and with α⁡(F∩∂jY)=μj\alpha(F\cap\partial_{j}Y)\mkern-1.5mu=\mkern-1.5mu\mu_{j} for each j∈J:={1,…,n}∖J¯j\mkern-2.0mu\in\mkern-2.0muJ\mkern-2.0mu:\mkern-0.3mu=\mkern-2.0mu\{1,\ldots,n\}\mkern-2.0mu\setminus\mkern-2.0mu\bar{J}, then Proposition 2.1 again allows us to isotop each separating torus ∂ȷ¯Y\partial_{\bar{\jmath}}Y so that FF restricts to a co-oriented taut foliation on YY, transverse to ∂Y\partial Y, with α⁡(F∩∂iY)=μi\alpha(F\cap\partial_{i}Y)\mkern-1.5mu=\mkern-1.5mu\mu_{i} for each i∈{1,…,n}i\mkern-2.0mu\in\mkern-2.0mu\{1,\ldots,n\}.

We then apply the the foliation gluing theorem of Boyer and Clay [4, Theorem 9.5.2]. That is, for each i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, Theorem 2.5 computes that ℱ⁡(N¯i)={li}\mathcal{F}(\bar{N}_{i})=\{l_{i}\}, with lil_{i} (of slope 00) the rational longitude of of the ithi^{\mathrm{th}} copy N¯i\bar{N}_{i} of N¯\bar{N}. Thus, for any gluing maps φi:N¯i→−∂iY\varphi_{i}:\bar{N}_{i}\to-\partial_{i}Y sending li↦μil_{i}\mapsto\mu_{i} in homology, Boyer’s and Clay’s gluing theorem tells us that there exist co-oriented taut foliations F′F^{\prime} on YY and FiF_{i} on N¯i\bar{N}_{i}, transverse to respective boundaries, with α(F′∩∂iY)=μi=φi∗ℙ(α(Fj∩∂N¯j))\alpha(F^{\prime}\cap\partial_{i}Y)\mkern-1.5mu=\mkern-1.5mu\mu_{i}\mkern-1.5mu=\mkern-1.5mu\varphi_{i*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(\alpha(F_{j}\cap\partial\bar{N}_{j})) for each i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, such that the FiF_{i} and F′F^{\prime} glue together to form a co-oriented taut foliation on the N¯\bar{N}-filling YN¯​(μ∗)Y^{\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\mu_{*}) specified by the φi\varphi_{i}. After isotoping the ∂iY\partial_{i}Y to be transverse to this foliation, we can restrict this foliation to any any sub-N¯\bar{N}-filling YN¯​(J¯′,μ∗)⊂YN¯​(μ∗)Y^{\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\bar{J}^{\prime};\mu_{*})\subset Y^{\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\mu_{*}). ∎

In particular, for a graph manifold YY with torus boundary, we have μ∈ℱ⁡(Y)\mu\in\mathcal{F}(Y) if and only if an N¯\bar{N}-filling YN¯​(μ)Y^{\mkern-1.0mu\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\mu) admits a co-oriented taut foliation.

3. L-space intervals

An L-space is a closed oriented three manifold whose Heegaard Floer homology is trivial, in the sense that for each Spinc\mathrm{Spin}^{c} structure, the hat Heegaard Floer homology looks like the singular homology of a point. The reader unfamiliar with L-spaces could consult [31, 32] for an introduction to Heegaard Floer homology, or [33] for a treatment of L-space Dehn fillings. For present purposes, we shall only need the classification of Seifert fibered L-spaces, some formal properties of sets of L-space Dehn-filling slopes, and some basic gluing results, all of which we catalog below.

3.1. L-space Dehn fillings and N¯\bar{N}-fillings

Definition 3.1.

If YY is a compact oriented three-manifold with torus boundary, then we define the L-space interval of YY to be

(25) ℒ⁡(Y):={μ∈ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y))|Y⁡(μ)​ is an L-space}.\mathcal{L}(Y):=\left\{\mu\in{\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y))|\,Y(\mu)\text{ is an L-space}\right\}.

We shall write ℒ∘​(Y)\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y) for the interior of ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) in ℙ​(H1​(∂Y)){\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)).

Thus, ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) is analogous to, and often complementary to, ℱD​(Y)\mathcal{F}^{D}(Y), especially when YY has no reducible non-L-space Dehn-fillings. Moreover, since the set of slopes of co-oriented taut foliations meeting a generalized rotation number condition is often the closure of the set of product foliation slopes meeting that condition [10, Lemma 3.31], it is natural to ask if ℱ⁡(Y)\mathcal{F}(Y) bears any relation to the complement of ℒ∘​(Y)\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y). In fact, we have the following result.

Proposition 3.2 ([33]).

If YY\mkern-2.5mu is a compact oriented three manifold with torus boundary, then an N¯\bar{N}-filling YN¯​(μ)Y^{\mkern-1.0mu\bar{N}}\mkern-2.0mu(\mu) is an L-space if and only if μ∈ℒ∘​(Y)\mu\in\mathcal{L}^{\circ}\mkern-2.0mu(Y).

Proof.

In [33, Proposition 7.9], J. Rasmussen and the author prove the above result with N¯\bar{N} replaced by any member of a more general class of manifolds dubbed generalized solid tori. Since N¯\bar{N} is a generalized solid torus as defined in [33], the result follows. ∎

Thus ℒ∘​(Y)\mathcal{L}^{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu(Y) can be regarded as the L-space N¯\bar{N}-filling interval of YY.

3.2. L-space gluing

Our primary tool for characterizing when a union of three-manifolds along a torus boundary gives an L-space is the following joint result of J. Rasmussen and the author [33]. Hanselman and Watson have proven a similar result in [19].

Proposition 3.3 ([33]).

If each of Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} is a compact oriented three-manifold with torus boundary, then for any gluing map φ:∂Y1→−∂Y2\varphi:\partial Y_{1}\to-\partial Y_{2} with φ∗ℙ​(ℒ∘​(Y1))∩ℒ∘​(Y2)≠∅\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{1}))\cap\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{2})\neq\emptyset, the union Y1∪φY2Y_{1}\cup_{\varphi}\!Y_{2} is an L-space if and only if ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y2))=φ∗ℙ​(ℒ∘​(Y1))∪ℒ∘​(Y2){\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y_{2}))=\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{1}))\cup\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{2}) if both YiY_{i} are boundary incompressible, and if and only if ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y2))=φ∗ℙ​(ℒ⁡(Y1))∪ℒ⁡(Y2){\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y_{2}))=\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{L}(Y_{1}))\cup\mathcal{L}(Y_{2}) otherwise.

Proof.

Recall that a compact three-manifold with torus boundary is boundary incompressible if and only if it is not a connected sum of a solid torus with a (possibly empty) closed three-manifold. The above proposition replicates Theorem 6.2 from [33], except with the hypothesis of boundary incompressibility of each YiY_{i} replacing an a priori more technical condition that certain subsets 𝒟τ​(Yi)⊂H1​(Yi)\mathcal{D}^{\tau}(Y_{i})\subset H_{1}(Y_{i}) be nonempty. Thomas Gillespie has recently shown [17] these two conditions to be equivalent. None of our gluing arguments involving graph manifolds actually make use of his result, but our later cabling results, which in principle require unions with non graph manifolds, do require Gillespie’s result.

∎

We shall later show that in the case of non-solid-torus graph manifolds YiY_{i} with torus boundary, various foliation results allow us to drop some of the above hypotheses, so that one obtains an L-space if and only if ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y2))=φ∗ℙ​(ℒ∘​(Y1))∪ℒ∘​(Y2){\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y_{2}))=\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{1}))\cup\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{2}).

In rather the opposite direction, if YY is Seifert fibered over a punctured S2S^{2} or ℝ​ℙ2{\mathbb{R}}{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, then a Dehn filling Y′Y^{\prime} of YY fails to be a graph manifold if and only if Y′Y^{\prime} fails to be prime, if and only if Y′≠S1×S2Y^{\prime}\neq S^{1}\times S^{2} and the Dehn filling, in some ∂iY\partial_{i}Y, was along the fiber lift f~i∈H1​(∂iY)\tilde{f}_{i}\in H_{1}(\partial_{i}Y) of slope πi​(f~i)=∞\pi_{i}(\tilde{f}_{i})=\infty (see the Remark in Section 2.2). In this case, Y′Y^{\prime} is neither a graph manifold nor a habitat for taut foliations, but since it has compressible boundary, its L-space gluing properties simplify, due to the following result.

Proposition 3.4.

Suppose that each of Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} is a compact oriented three-manifold with torus boundary, and that Y1Y_{1} has compressible boundary. Then the union Y1∪φY2Y_{1}\cup_{\varphi}\!Y_{2} is an L-space if and only if X1,…,XNX_{1},\ldots,X_{N} are all L-spaces and φ∗ℙ​(l1)∈ℒ⁡(Y2)\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(l_{1})\in\mathcal{L}(Y_{2}), where l1l_{1} is the rational longitude of Y1Y_{1}, and where Y1Y_{1} decomposes as Y1=(S1×D2)#(X1#⋯#XN)Y_{1}=(S^{1}\mkern-1.5mu\times\mkern-1.5muD^{2})\#(X_{1}\#\cdots\#X_{N}).

Proof.

A union along toroidal boundaries with a solid torus is just a Dehn filling, so we have Y1∪φY2=Y2(φ∗ℙ(l1))#X1#⋯#XNY_{1}\cup_{\varphi}\!Y_{2}=Y_{2}(\varphi^{{\mathbb{P}}}_{*}(l_{1}))\#X_{1}\#\cdots\#X_{N}, and a connected sum of closed manifolds is an L-space if and only if each summand is an L-space. ∎

The above result explains why not every graph manifold YY with torus boundary satisfies ℱD​(Y)∐ℒ⁡(Y)=ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y))\mathcal{F}^{D}(Y)\amalg\mathcal{L}(Y)={\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)). That is, no reducible manifold (besides S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2}) admits a co-oriented taut foliation, but there exist graph manifolds with reducible Dehn fillings which are not S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2} or an L-space.

3.3. Floer simple manifolds and L-space intervals

It is not known, in general, what forms the sets ℱ⁡(Y)\mathcal{F}(Y) or ℱD​(Y)\mathcal{F}^{D}(Y) can take for an arbitrary compact oriented three-manifold YY with torus boundary, but the situation for L-spaces is better understood. As shown in [33] by J. Rasmussen and the author, ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) can only be empty, the set of a single point, a closed interval, or the complement of the rational longitude in ℙ​(H1​(∂Y)){\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)). For historical reasons, we call YY Floer simple in the latter two cases. Equivalently, we could define Floer simple manifolds as follows.

Definition 3.5.

A compact oriented three-manifold YY with torus boundary is Floer simple if ℒ∘​(Y)≠∅\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y)\neq\emptyset.

In particular, if YY is Floer simple, then its space ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) of L-space Dehn filling slopes can be specified entirely in terms of the left-hand and right-hand endpoints of ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y), in a sense we can make precise, prefaced with the introduction of an abbreviative notation for the closed interval with infinite endpoint.

Definition 3.6.

For y∈ℚy\in{\mathbb{Q}}, we shall write [−∞,y][-\infty,y], [y,+∞][y,+\infty], [−∞,y⟩\left[-\infty,y\right>, and ⟨y,+∞]\left<y,+\infty\right] for the following intervals in (ℚ∪{∞})⊂(ℝ∪{∞})({\mathbb{Q}}\cup\{\infty\})\subset({\mathbb{R}}\cup\{\infty\}):

[−∞,y]\displaystyle[-\infty,y] :={∞}∪⟨−∞,y],\displaystyle:=\{\infty\}\cup\left<-\infty,y\right], [−∞,y⟩\displaystyle\left[-\infty,y\right> :={∞}∪⟨−∞,y⟩,\displaystyle:=\{\infty\}\cup\left<-\infty,y\right>,
[y,+∞]\displaystyle[y,+\infty] :=[y,+∞⟩∪{∞},\displaystyle:=\left[y,+\infty\right>\cup\{\infty\}, ⟨y,+∞]\displaystyle\left<y,+\infty\right] :=⟨y,+∞⟩∪{∞}.\displaystyle:=\left<y,+\infty\right>\cup\{\infty\}.
Definition 3.7.

If y−,y+∈ℚ∪{∞}y_{-},y_{+}\!\in{\mathbb{Q}}\cup\{\infty\}, then we define the L-space interval from y−y_{-} to y+y_{+}, denoted [[y−,y+]]⊂ℚ∪{∞}[[y_{-},y_{+}]]\subset{\mathbb{Q}}\cup\{\infty\}, as follows:

(26) [[y−,y+]]:={⟨−∞,+∞⟩∞=y−,y+=∞⟨y−,+∞]∪[−∞,y+⟩ℚ∋y−=y+∈ℚ[y−,+∞]∪[−∞,y+]ℚ∋y−>y+∈ℚ[y−,+∞]∩[−∞,y+]ℚ∋y−<y+∈ℚ[−∞,y+]∞=y−,y+∈ℚ[y−,+∞]ℚ∋y−,y+=∞.[[y_{-},y_{+}]]:=\begin{cases}\left<-\infty,+\infty\right>&\infty\mkern-1.5mu=\mkern-1.5muy_{-}\mkern 8.2mu,\mkern 8.3muy_{+}\mkern-1.5mu=\mkern-1.5mu\infty\\ \left<y_{-},+\infty\right]\cup\left[-\infty,y_{+}\right>&\,{\mathbb{Q}}\ni y_{-}=y_{+}\in{\mathbb{Q}}\\ [y_{-},+\infty]\cup[-\infty,y_{+}]&\,{\mathbb{Q}}\ni y_{-}>y_{+}\in{\mathbb{Q}}\\ [y_{-},+\infty]\cap[-\infty,y_{+}]&\,{\mathbb{Q}}\ni y_{-}<y_{+}\in{\mathbb{Q}}\\ [-\infty,y_{+}]&\infty\mkern-1.5mu=\mkern-1.5muy_{-}\mkern 8.2mu,\mkern 8.3muy_{+}\in{\mathbb{Q}}\\ [y_{-},+\infty]&\,{\mathbb{Q}}\ni y_{-}\mkern 8.2mu,\mkern 8.3muy_{+}\mkern-1.5mu=\mkern-1.5mu\infty\end{cases}.

In other words, [[y−,y+]][[y_{-},y_{+}]] is the unique interval with left-hand endpoint y−y_{-} and right-hand endpoint y+y_{+} which is closed if y−≠y+y_{-}\neq y_{+} and open otherwise.

Remark: In practice, we extend the above definition to allow y−=−∞y_{-}=-\infty or y+=+∞y_{+}=+\infty, which we treat as identical to the respective cases of y−=∞y_{-}=\infty or y+=∞y_{+}=\infty.

Proposition 3.8.

Suppose, for some compact oriented three-manifold YY with torus boundary, that we are given an identification ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y))≅ℚ∪{∞}{\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y))\cong{\mathbb{Q}}\cup\{\infty\}. If YY is Floer simple, then there are unique y−,y+∈ℚ∪{∞}y_{-},y_{+}\!\in{\mathbb{Q}}\cup\{\infty\} such that ℒ⁡(Y)=[[y−,y+]]⊂ℚ∪{∞}\mathcal{L}(Y)=[[y_{-},y_{+}]]\subset{\mathbb{Q}}\cup\{\infty\}. Conversely, if there are y−,y+∈ℚ∪{∞}y_{-},y_{+}\!\in{\mathbb{Q}}\cup\{\infty\} for which ℒ⁡(Y)=[[y−,y+]]\mathcal{L}(Y)=[[y_{-},y_{+}]], then YY is Floer simple.

The above follows from the aforementioned result, proven in [33], that if ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) contains more than one point, then ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) is either a closed interval or the complement of a point in ℙ​(H1​(∂Y)){\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)). The following computation of L-space intervals for Seifert fibered spaces demonstrates one use of this “[[⋅,⋅]][[\cdot\mkern 0.7mu,\mkern-0.8mu\cdot]]” notation.

Proposition 3.9.

If YY is a regular fiber complement in a Seifert fibered rational homology sphere, then ℒ∘​(Y)∐ℱ⁡(Y)=ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y))\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y)\amalg\mathcal{F}(Y)={\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)). If YY has non-orientable base, we have ℒ⁡(Y)=⟨−∞,+∞⟩\mathcal{L}(Y)=\left<-\infty,+\infty\right> and ℱD​(Y)=∅\mathcal{F}^{D}\mkern-2.0mu(Y)=\emptyset (unless YY is the twisted S2S^{2}-bundle over the Möbius strip, in which case ℱD​(Y)={∞}\mathcal{F}^{D}\mkern-2.0mu(Y)\mkern-2.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu\{\infty\}) If YY is a regular fiber complement in MS2​(y∗)M_{S^{2}}(y_{*}), for some y∗=(y0,…,yn)∈ℚn+1y_{*}=(y_{0},\ldots,y_{n})\in{\mathbb{Q}}^{n+1}, then ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y))∖ℱD​(Y)=ℒ⁡(Y)=[[y−,y+]]{\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y))\setminus\mathcal{F}^{D}(Y)=\mathcal{L}(Y)=[[y_{-},y_{+}]], where

(27) y−:=maxk>0−1k​(1+∑i=0n⌊yi​k⌋),y+:=mink>0−1k​(−1+∑i=0n⌈yi​k⌉),y_{-}:=\max_{k>0}-\mathord{\raise 0.49991pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.4pt}{}{1}{k}$}}\mkern-1.8mu\left(\mkern 2.0mu1+{{\textstyle{\sum\limits_{i=0}^{n}\left\lfloor y_{i}k\right\rfloor}}}\right),\;\;\;\;\;y_{+}:=\min_{k>0}-\mathord{\raise 0.49991pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.4pt}{}{1}{k}$}}\mkern-1.8mu\left(\mkern-3.0mu-1+{{\textstyle{\sum\limits_{i=0}^{n}\left\lceil y_{i}k\right\rceil}}}\right),

unless YY\mkern-4.5mu is a solid torus, in which case y−:=y+:=−∑i=0nyiy_{-}\mkern-3.2mu:\mkern-0.3mu=\mkern-1.0muy_{+}\mkern-3.2mu:\mkern-0.3mu=\mkern-1.0mu-\mkern-3.5mu\sum_{i=0}^{n}y_{i} is the rational longitude of YY\mkern-5.0mu.

Proof.

For the case of YY with non-orientable base, see the work of Boyer, Gordon, and Watson [5] and Boyer and Clay [4]. For YY with orientable base, the foliations result is due to Jankins, Neumann, and Naimi [23, 28], and the L-space result is originally due to the combined work of Jankins, Neumann, and Naimi [23, 28], Eliashberg and Thurston [13], Ozsváth and Szabó [30], Lisca and Matić [26], and Lisca and Stipsicz [27]. Alternatively, J. Rasmussen and the author offer a recent stand-alone proof of the L-space result [33]. ∎

4. L-space Intervals and Foliation Slopes for Graph Manifolds

This is the section in which we prove most of our main results. We begin, however, by introducing the notion of L/NTF-equivalence, the presence of which makes gluing easier. We further pause in Section 4.2, to establish some conventions for graph manifolds with torus boundary and b1=1b_{1}=1.

4.1. L/NTF-equivalence and Gluing

For a pair of manifolds spliced together along torus boundaries, we can often prove stronger gluing results about the existence of co-oriented taut foliations or non-trivial Heegaard Floer homology if we are able to use gluing theorems from both areas of mathematics. In general, however, this strategy only works if we know that each manifold behaves in a suitably complementary manner with respect to co-oriented taut foliations and L-space Dehn fillings, a notion which we now make precise.

Definition 4.1.

If YY\! is a prime compact oriented three-manifold with torus boundary, then we call YY L/NTF-equivalent if ℱ⁡(Y)∐ℒ∘​(Y)=ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y))\mathcal{F}(Y)\amalg\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y)={\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)).

In certain circumstances, one can characterize L/NTF-equivalence in terms of N¯\bar{N}-fillings.

Proposition 4.2.

Suppose YY\! is a prime compact oriented three-manifold with torus boundary. If b1​(Y)>1b_{1}(Y)>1 or YY is a graph manifold, then YY\! is L/NTF-equivalent if and only if each N¯\bar{N}-filling of YY\! is an L-space precisely when it fails to admit a co-oriented taut foliation.

Proof.

This follows immediately from Propositions 2.8 and 3.2. ∎

There are some classes of manifold which we already know to be L/NTF-equivalent.

Proposition 4.3.

Suppose YY is a prime compact oriented three-manifold with torus boundary. If b1​(Y)>1b_{1}(Y)>1, or if YY is the union of a Seifert fibered space with zero or more copies of N¯\bar{N}, then YY is L/NTF-equivalent.

Proof.

If b1​(Y)>1b_{1}(Y)\mkern-2.0mu>\mkern-2.0mu1, then since no Dehn filling of YY is a rational homology sphere, we have ℒ⁡(Y)=∅\mathcal{L}(Y)\mkern-2.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu\emptyset, implying ℒ∘​(Y)=∅\mathcal{L}^{\circ}\mkern-2.0mu(Y)\mkern-2.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu\emptyset. Correspondingly, Proposition 2.8 implies ℱ⁡(Y)=ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y))\mathcal{F}(Y)\mkern-2.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu{\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)).

Suppose YY has b1​(Y)=1b_{1}(Y)=1 and is the union of a Seifert fibered space with zero or more copies of N¯\bar{N}. Then, using [33, Proposition 7.9] of J. Rasmussen and the author to replace Boyer’s and Clay’s “NtN_{t}” manifolds with N¯\bar{N}, we invoke the “slope detection” theorem of Boyer and Clay [4, Theorem 8.1] to deduce L/NTF-equivalence for YY.

Alternatively, one could prove the same result by inductively performing N¯\bar{N}-fillings in regular fiber complements, starting with Proposition 3.9 for the Seifert fibered base case, and using the gluing result in Proposition 4.4 below, together with (21) and (22), to evolve (27) to match (23). Similar inductive arguments appear in the proof of Theorem 4.6. ∎

Remark. We later prove L/NTF-equivalence for all graph manifolds with torus boundary.

We are now ready to state our main gluing result.

Proposition 4.4.

Suppose Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} are non-solid-torus L/NTF-equivalent graph manifolds with torus boundary. Then for any union Y1∪φY2Y_{1}\cup_{\varphi}\!Y_{2}, φ:∂Y1→−∂Y2\varphi:\partial Y_{1}\to-\partial Y_{2}, the following are equivalent:

  1. (i)(i)\phantom{ii}

    Y1∪φY2Y_{1}\cup_{\varphi}\!Y_{2} is an L-space.

  2. (i​i)(ii)\phantom{i}

    Y1∪φY2Y_{1}\cup_{\varphi}\!Y_{2} does not admit a co-oriented taut foliation.

  3. (i​i​i)(iii)

    φ∗ℙ​(ℒ∘​(Y1))∪ℒ∘​(Y2)=ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y2))\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{1}))\cup\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{2})={\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y_{2})).

Proof.

Suppose (i​i​i)(iii) holds, so that Proposition 3.3 implies Y1∪φY2Y_{1}\cup_{\varphi}\!Y_{2} is an L-space. Ozsváth and Szabó have shown [30] that an L-space does not admit C2C^{2} co-oriented taut foliations, and this result has been improved to C0C^{0} co-oriented taut foliations by Bowden [3] and independently by Kazez and Roberts [24].

Suppose (i​i​i)(iii) fails to hold. If b1(Y1∪φY2)>0b_{1}(Y_{1}\mkern 1.5mu\cup_{\varphi}\mkern-1.5muY_{2})\mkern-1.0mu>\mkern-1.0mu0, then Gabai [14] tells us there is a co-oriented taut foliation on Y1∪φY2Y_{1}\cup_{\varphi}\mkern-1.5muY_{2}, and we also know that Y1∪φY2Y_{1}\cup_{\varphi}\mkern-2.0muY_{2} is not an L-space. Suppose instead that b1(Y1∪φY2)=0b_{1}(Y_{1}\mkern 1.5mu\cup_{\varphi}\mkern-1.5muY_{2})=0. Then L/NTF-equivalence implies φ∗ℙ​(ℱ⁡(Y1))∩ℱ⁡(Y2)≠∅\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{F}(Y_{1}))\cap\mathcal{F}(Y_{2})\neq\emptyset, and so there are co-oriented taut foliations FiF_{i} on YiY_{i} transverse to ∂Yi\partial Y_{i} such that φ∗ℙ​(α⁡(F1∩∂Y1))=α⁡(F2∩∂Y2)\varphi^{{\mathbb{P}}}_{*}(\alpha(F_{1}\cap\partial Y_{1}))=\alpha(F_{2}\cap\partial Y_{2}). By Corollary 2.2, we can isotop the incompressible tori in Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} so that each FiF_{i} restricts to boundary-transverse co-oriented taut foliations on each of the JSJ components of each YiY_{i}. This means that the JSJ components of Y1∪φY2Y_{1}\cup_{\varphi}\mkern-2.0muY_{2} each admit boundary-transverse co-oriented taut foliations which restrict to boundary foliations of matching slopes with respect to boundary-gluing maps. We can therefore invoke the foliation gluing theorem of Boyer and Clay [4, Theorem 9.5.2] to assert the existence of a co-oriented taut foliation on all of Y1∪φY2Y_{1}\cup_{\varphi}\mkern-2.0muY_{2}. Again, this co-oriented taut foliation implies that Y1∪φY2Y_{1}\cup_{\varphi}\!Y_{2} is not an L-space. ∎

4.2. Graph manifold conventions

Any closed graph manifold can be regarded as a Dehn filling of a graph manifold YY with torus boundary. If b1​(Y)>1b_{1}(Y)>1, then ℒ⁡(Y)=ℒ∘​(Y)=∅\mathcal{L}(Y)=\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y)=\emptyset and ℱ⁡(Y)=ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y))\mathcal{F}(Y)={\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)) (see Proposition 4.3), which is not very interesting.

If b1​(Y)=1b_{1}(Y)=1, then we call YY a tree manifold, since YY admits a rational homology sphere Dehn filling, corresponding to a tree graph. Rooting the tree graph for YY at the Seifert fibered piece containing ∂Y\partial Y provides a recursive construction for YY,

4.3. Statement of Main Results

We first show that all graph manifolds with torus boundary are L/NTF-equivalent, making our main gluing tool, Proposition 4.4, applicable for all such non-solid-torus graph manifolds. We then can make the inductive gluing arguments necessary to calculate L-space intervals for graph manifolds with torus boundary.

Theorem 4.5.

Every graph manifold YY with torus boundary is L/NTF equivalent, i.e., satisfies ℱ⁡(Y)∐ℒ∘​(Y)=ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y))\mathcal{F}(Y)\amalg\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y)={\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)). Moreover, if we let ℛ⁡(Y)\mathcal{R}(Y)\! denote the set of slopes of reducible (and not S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2}) Dehn fillings of YY\!, then ℱD​(Y)∐(ℒ⁡(Y)∪ℛ⁡(Y))=ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y))\mathcal{F}^{D}(Y)\amalg(\mathcal{L}(Y)\cup\mathcal{R}(Y))={\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)).

The above also implies that the following calculation of ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) for graph manifolds YY\! with torus boundary completely determines both ℱ⁡(Y)\mathcal{F}(Y) and ℱD​(Y)\mathcal{F}^{D}(Y).

Theorem 4.6.

Suppose YY is a graph manifold with torus boundary and nonempty ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y). If the Seifert fibered component of YY containing ∂Y\partial Y has non-orientable base, then ℒ⁡(Y)=⟨−∞,+∞⟩\mathcal{L}(Y)=\left<-\infty,+\infty\right>. Otherwise, we have

ℒ⁡(Y)={[[y−,y+]]Y​Floer simple,{y−}={y+}Y​not Floer simple,\mathcal{L}(Y)=\begin{cases}[[y_{-},y_{+}]]&\;\;\;Y\,\text{Floer simple},\\ \{y_{-}\}=\{y_{+}\}&\;\;\;Y\,\text{not Floer simple},\end{cases}

where, for nd,ng,yid,yi−g,n_{{\textsc{d}}},n_{{\textsc{g}}},y_{i}^{\textsc{d}},y_{i-}^{\textsc{g}}\mkern-0.2mu,\mkern-1.0mu and yi+gy_{i+}^{\textsc{g}}\mkern-3.0mu as defined in Section 4.2, we define y−,y+∈ℚ∪{∞}y_{-},y_{+}\in{\mathbb{Q}}\cup\{\infty\} as

y−\displaystyle y_{-} :=maxk>0−1k​(1+∑i=1nd⌊yid​k⌋+∑i=1ng(⌈yi+g​k⌉−1)),\displaystyle:=\,\max_{k>0}-\mathord{\raise 0.49991pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.4pt}{}{1}{k}$}}\mkern-2.5mu\left(1+{{\textstyle{\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n_{{\textsc{d}}}}\left\lfloor y^{\textsc{d}}_{i}k\right\rfloor}}}+{{\textstyle{\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n_{{\textsc{g}}}}\left(\left\lceil y^{\textsc{g}}_{i+}k\right\rceil-1\right)}}}\right),

unless YY\! is a solid torus, in which case y−:=y+:=−∑i=1ndyidy_{-}\!:=\mkern-2.0muy_{+}\!:=\mkern-2.0mu-\sum_{i=1}^{n_{{\textsc{d}}}}y_{i}^{\textsc{d}}.

In particular, the maximum (respectively, minimum) is realized for k≤s±k\leq s_{\pm}, where s±s_{\pm} is the least common positive multiple of the denominators of y1d,…,ynddy_{1}^{\textsc{d}},\ldots,y_{n_{{\textsc{d}}}}^{\textsc{d}} and y1±g,…,yng±gy_{1\pm}^{\textsc{g}},\ldots,y_{n_{{\textsc{g}}}\pm}^{\textsc{g}}, with ∓\mp and ±\pm cases taken respectively from top to bottom. Unlike the case of oriented Seifert fibered spaces over the Möbius strip or disk, not all graph manifolds with torus boundary are Floer simple. We therefore need a companion result to characterize precisely when ℒ∘\mathcal{L}^{\circ} or ℒ\mathcal{L} is nonempty.

∞∈ℒ⁡(Y)\infty\mkern-1.5mu\in\mkern-1.5mu\mathcal{L}(Y)\mkern-1.0mu if and only if either condition (fs3)(\textsc{fs3}\mkern-0.5mu) from Proposition 4.7 holds, in which case ∞∈ℒ⁡(Y)=[[y−,y+]]\infty\mkern-2.0mu\in\mkern-2.0mu\mathcal{L}(Y)\mkern-2.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu[[y_{-},y_{+}]], or condition (nfs3)(\textsc{nfs3}\mkern-0.5mu) or (nfs4)(\textsc{nfs4}\mkern-0.5mu) from Proposition 4.7 holds, in which case ℒ⁡(Y)={y−}={y+}={∞}\mathcal{L}(Y)=\{y_{-}\}=\{y_{+}\}=\{\infty\}.

Conditions (nfs3)(\textsc{nfs3}\mkern-0.5mu) and (fs3)(\textsc{fs3}\mkern-0.5mu) jointly exhaust the cases in which the right-hand condition of (55) holds and all daughter subtrees Y1,…,YngY_{1},\dots,Y_{n_{{\textsc{g}}}} are Floer simple. Condition (nfs4)(\textsc{nfs4}\mkern-0.5mu), on the other hand, describes all cases in which the the right-hand condition of (55) holds and at least one YjY_{j} is not Floer simple.

If (nfs4)(\textsc{nfs4}\mkern-0.5mu) holds, then, permuting the daughter subtrees without loss of generality so that φng∗ℙ(ℒ(Yng))={∞}\varphi^{{\mathbb{P}}}_{n_{{\textsc{g}}}*}(\mathcal{L}(Y_{n_{{\textsc{g}}}}))\mkern-2.5mu=\mkern-2.5mu\{\infty\}, we have ℒ∘​(Yng)=∅\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{n_{{\textsc{g}}}})\mkern-2.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu\emptyset, which, by (40), implies ℒ⁡(Y)∩ℚ=∅\mathcal{L}(Y)\cap{\mathbb{Q}}\mkern-2.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu\emptyset, so that ℒ⁡(Y)={∞}\mathcal{L}(Y)\mkern-2.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu\{\infty\}. Proposition 4.9.

Suppose ∞∉ℒ⁡(Y)\infty\notin\mathcal{L}(Y). Then ℒ⁡(Y)≠∅\mathcal{L}(Y)\neq\emptyset if and only if either (nfs2)(\textsc{nfs2}\mkern-0.5mu) holds for YY, in which case ℒ⁡(Y)={y−}={y+}\mathcal{L}(Y)=\{y_{-}\}=\{y_{+}\}, or (fs1)(\textsc{fs1}\mkern-0.5mu) or (fs2)(\textsc{fs2}\mkern-0.5mu) holds for YY, in which case ℒ⁡(Y)=[[y−,y+]]\mathcal{L}(Y)=[[y_{-},y_{+}]].

Proof.

We first observe that if any daughter subtree of YY fails to be Floer simple, then ℒ⁡(Y)=∅\mathcal{L}(Y)=\emptyset. ∎

(82) {[[y^−,y^+]]∘∪[[y1−g,y1+g]]∘=ℚ∪{∞}if​Y^​[y]​has incompressible boundaryy^−=y^+∈[[y1−g,y1+g]]if​Y^​[y]​has compressible boundary.\begin{cases}[[\hat{y}_{-},\hat{y}_{+}]]^{\circ}\cup[[y_{1-}^{\textsc{g}},y_{1+}^{\textsc{g}}]]^{\circ}={\mathbb{Q}}\cup\{\infty\}&\;\;\;\;\text{if}\;\hat{Y}[y]\;\text{has incompressible boundary}\\ \hat{y}_{-}=\hat{y}_{+}\in[[y_{1-}^{\textsc{g}},y_{1+}^{\textsc{g}}]]&\;\;\;\;\text{if}\;\hat{Y}[y]\;\text{has compressible boundary}.\end{cases}

Proposition 4.11.

Suppose Y1Y_{1} is Floer simple. Then ∞∈ℒ⁡(Y)\infty\mkern-2.0mu\in\mkern-2.0mu\mathcal{L}(Y) if and only if condition (fs3)(\textsc{fs3}\mkern-0.5mu) from Proposition 4.7 holds, in which case ℒ⁡(Y)=[[y−,y+]]\mathcal{L}(Y)\mkern-2.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu[[y_{-},y_{+}]].

For the remainder of the proof, we assume (fs3)(\textsc{fs3}\mkern-0.5mu) holds.

Consider the case in which y1−g≠y1+gy_{1-}^{\textsc{g}}\mkern-4.0mu\neq\mkern-1.5muy_{1+}^{\textsc{g}}. Thus, for y∈ℚy\in{\mathbb{Q}}, the condition y∈[[y−,y+]]y\in[[y_{-},y_{+}]] is respectively equivalent to the right-hand conditions of (a) (70), (b) (71), or (c) (70) or (71) from Claim 3, each of which conditions, given the respective form of [[y1−g,y1+g]][[y_{1-}^{\textsc{g}},y_{1+}^{\textsc{g}}]], is equivalent to (82), which holds if and only if Y⁡(y)Y(y) is and L-space, and we conclude that ℒ⁡(Y)=[[y−,y+]]\mathcal{L}(Y)=[[y_{-},y_{+}]].

(83) y∈ℒ⁡(Y)⇔{y1g∈[[y^−,y^+]]∘{y1d,y}∩ℤ=∅y≠−y1d−y1g{y1d,y}∩ℤ≠∅.y\in\mathcal{L}(Y)\;\;\iff\;\;\begin{cases}y_{1}^{\textsc{g}}\in[[\hat{y}_{-},\hat{y}_{+}]]^{\circ}&\{y_{1}^{\textsc{d}},y\}\cap{\mathbb{Z}}=\emptyset\\ y\neq-y_{1}^{\textsc{d}}-y_{1}^{\textsc{g}}&\{y_{1}^{\textsc{d}},y\}\cap{\mathbb{Z}}\neq\emptyset.\end{cases}

The derivation of the {y1d,y}∩ℤ=∅\{y_{1}^{\textsc{d}},y\}\cap{\mathbb{Z}}=\emptyset case from (82) is immediate. In the {y1d,y}∩ℤ≠∅\{y_{1}^{\textsc{d}},y\}\cap{\mathbb{Z}}\neq\emptyset case, (82) tells us that y∈ℒ⁡(Y)y\in\mathcal{L}(Y) if and only if y^−≠y1d\hat{y}_{-}\mkern-2.5mu\neq\mkern-0.5muy_{1}^{\textsc{d}}. Now, since (fs3)(\textsc{fs3}\mkern-0.5mu) demands that ∞∈[[y1−g,y1+g]]\infty\in[[y_{1-}^{\textsc{g}},y_{1+}^{\textsc{g}}]], implying y1g∈ℚy_{1}^{\textsc{g}}\mkern-2.5mu\in\mkern-1.0mu{\mathbb{Q}}, Claim 4 tells us that y+≤−y1d−y1g≤y−y_{+}\mkern 0.5mu\leq-y_{1}^{\textsc{d}}\mkern-1.5mu-\mkern-1.1muy_{1}^{\textsc{g}}\mkern 2.0mu\leq\mkern 2.0muy_{-}, with y−=y+y_{-}\mkern-3.0mu=\mkern-1.5muy_{+} if and only if y1d∈ℤ\mkern 0.5muy_{1}^{\textsc{d}}\in{\mathbb{Z}}\mkern 0.5mu or y1d+y1g∈ℤ\mkern 0.5muy_{1}^{\textsc{d}}\mkern-1.5mu+\mkern-0.8muy_{1}^{\textsc{g}}\in{\mathbb{Z}}. If y1d∈ℤ\mkern 0.5muy_{1}^{\textsc{d}}\in{\mathbb{Z}}\mkern 0.5mu, then (83) implies ℒ⁡(Y)=ℚ∪{∞}∖{−y1d−y1g}=[[y−,y+]]\mathcal{L}(Y)={\mathbb{Q}}\cup\{\infty\}\setminus\{-y_{1}^{\textsc{d}}-y_{1}^{\textsc{g}}\}=[[y_{-},y_{+}]]. (84) −⌈y1d+y1g⌉≤y+<−y1d−y1g<y−≤−⌊y1d+y1g⌋,-\lceil y_{1}^{\textsc{d}}\mkern-1.5mu+\mkern-1.1muy_{1}^{\textsc{g}}\rceil\mkern 2.0mu\leq\mkern 3.0muy_{+}\mkern 1.5mu<\mkern 1.0mu-y_{1}^{\textsc{d}}\mkern-1.5mu-\mkern-1.1muy_{1}^{\textsc{g}}\mkern 2.0mu<\mkern 3.0muy_{-}\mkern 1.5mu\leq\mkern 1.0mu-\lfloor y_{1}^{\textsc{d}}\mkern-1.5mu+\mkern-1.1muy_{1}^{\textsc{g}}\rfloor,

we observe that the complement of [[y−,y+]][[y_{-},y_{+}]] contains no integers, and so ℤ⊂[[y−,y+]]{\mathbb{Z}}\subset[[y_{-},y_{+}]]. On the other hand, for any y∈ℚ∖ℤy\in{\mathbb{Q}}\setminus{\mathbb{Z}}, (83) tells us that y∈ℒ⁡(Y)y\in\mathcal{L}(Y) if and only if y1g∈[[y^−,y^+]]∘y_{1}^{\textsc{g}}\in[[\hat{y}_{-},\hat{y}_{+}]]^{\circ}, which, by Claim 3, occurs if and only if y∈[y−,+∞]∪[−∞,y+]=[[y−,y+]]y\in[y_{-},+\infty]\cup[-\infty,y_{+}]=[[y_{-},y_{+}]]. Thus, once again, ℒ⁡(Y)=[[y−,y+]]\mathcal{L}(Y)=[[y_{-},y_{+}]], completing the proof of the proposition. ∎

Proposition 4.12.

Suppose Y1Y_{1} is Floer simple and ∞∉ℒ⁡(Y)\infty\mkern-1.0mu\notin\mkern-1.0mu\mathcal{L}(Y). Then ℒ⁡(Y)≠∅\mathcal{L}(Y)\mkern-1.8mu\neq\mkern-1.0mu\emptyset if and only if either condition (nfs2)(\textsc{nfs2}\mkern-0.5mu) from Proposition 4.7 holds, in which case ℒ⁡(Y)={y−}={y+}\mathcal{L}(Y)\mkern-2.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu\{y_{-}\}\mkern-2.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu\{y_{+}\}, or condition (fs1)(\textsc{fs1}\mkern-0.5mu) or (fs2)(\textsc{fs2}\mkern-0.5mu) holds, in which case ℒ⁡(Y)=[[y−,y+]]\mathcal{L}(Y)\mkern-2.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu[[y_{-},y_{+}]].

Proof.

Since Y1Y_{1} is Floer simple, and since ∞∉ℒ⁡(Y)\infty\mkern-1.0mu\notin\mkern-1.0mu\mathcal{L}(Y) implies that (fs3)(\textsc{fs3}\mkern-0.5mu) fails to hold, we know that ∞∉[[y1−g,y1+g]]\infty\notin[[y_{1-}^{\textsc{g}},y_{1+}^{\textsc{g}}]]. Thus, [[y1−g,y1+g]]=⟨−∞,+∞⟩[[y_{1-}^{\textsc{g}},y_{1+}^{\textsc{g}}]]=\left<-\infty,+\infty\right> or [[y1−g,y1+g]]=[y1−g,y1+g][[y_{1-}^{\textsc{g}},y_{1+}^{\textsc{g}}]]=[y_{1-}^{\textsc{g}},y_{1+}^{\textsc{g}}].

Suppose that [[y1−g,y1+g]]=⟨−∞,+∞⟩[[y_{1-}^{\textsc{g}},y_{1+}^{\textsc{g}}]]=\left<-\infty,+\infty\right>, which occurs if and only if condition (fs1)(\textsc{fs1}\mkern-0.5mu) holds. For any y∈ℚy\in{\mathbb{Q}}, we have ∞≠y^−≥y^+≠∞\infty\neq\hat{y}_{-}\geq\hat{y}_{+}\neq\infty, implying condition (82) holds, making Y⁡(y)Y\mkern-1.5mu(y) an L-space. Thus, since y1−g=y1+g=∞y_{1-}^{\textsc{g}}=y_{1+}^{\textsc{g}}=\infty implies y−=y+=∞y_{-}=y_{+}=\infty, we have ℒ⁡(Y)=ℚ=⟨−∞,+∞⟩=[[y−,y+]]\mathcal{L}(Y)={\mathbb{Q}}=\left<-\infty,+\infty\right>=[[y_{-},y_{+}]].

Lastly, suppose [[y1−g,y1+g]]=[y1−g,y1+g][[y_{1-}^{\textsc{g}},y_{1+}^{\textsc{g}}]]=[y_{1-}^{\textsc{g}},y_{1+}^{\textsc{g}}]. For any y∈ℚy\in{\mathbb{Q}}, we have y∈[y−,+∞]∩[−∞,y+]y\in[y_{-},+\infty]\cap[-\infty,y_{+}] if and only if the right-hand conditions of (70) and (71) from Claim 3 hold, which, since [[y1−g,y1+g]]=[y1−g,+∞]∩[y1−g,y1+g]≠∅[[y_{1-}^{\textsc{g}},y_{1+}^{\textsc{g}}]]=[y_{1-}^{\textsc{g}},+\infty]\cap[y_{1-}^{\textsc{g}},y_{1+}^{\textsc{g}}]\neq\emptyset, occurs if and only if (82) holds, which happens precisely when Y⁡(y)Y(y) is an L-space. Thus, ℒ⁡(Y)=[y−,+∞]∩[−∞,y+]\mathcal{L}(Y)=[y_{-},+\infty]\cap[-\infty,y_{+}], or in other words,

(85) ℒ⁡(Y)={[[y−,y+]]y−<y+{y−}={y+}y−=y+∅y−>y+.\mathcal{L}(Y)=\begin{cases}[[y_{-},y_{+}]]&y_{-}<y_{+}\\ \{y_{-}\}=\{y_{+}\}&y_{-}=y_{+}\\ \emptyset&y_{-}>y_{+}\end{cases}.

That is, ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) is nonempty if and only if either (fs2)(\textsc{fs2}\mkern-0.5mu) holds, in which case ℒ⁡(Y)=[[y−,y+]]\mathcal{L}(Y)=[[y_{-},y_{+}]], or (nfs2)(\textsc{nfs2}\mkern-0.5mu) holds, in which case ℒ⁡(Y)={y−}={y+}\mathcal{L}(Y)\!=\!\{y_{-}\}\!=\!\{y_{+}\}. ∎

The combined results of Sections 4.6, 4.7, and 4.8 prove that Theorem 4.6 and Proposition 4.7 hold for any graph manifold YY with torus boundary, b1=1b_{1}=1, tree height k>0k>0, and ng>0n_{{\textsc{g}}}>0 daughter subtrees, given the inductive assumptions, laid out in Section 4.5, that Theorem 4.6 and Proposition 4.7 hold for any graph manifold with torus boundary, b1=1b_{1}=1, and either tree height kk and ≤ng−1\leq n_{{\textsc{g}}}-1 daughter subtrees, or tree height ≤k−1\leq k-1.

For graph manifolds YY with torus boundary, b1=1b_{1}=1, and tree height kk, inducting on the number of daughter subtrees ngn_{{\textsc{g}}} yields the result that any graph manifold with torus boundary, b1=1b_{1}=1, and tree height kk satisfies Theorem 4.6 and Proposition 4.7. Inducting on tree height kk then completes the proof of Theorem 4.6 and Proposition 4.7.

5.4. Knots in L-spaces

It is possible to prove an analogous result for boundary incompressible Floer simple knot complements in arbitrary L-spaces.

To simplify the statement of such a result, we discard cables with p=0p=0, p=1p=1, or q=0q=0, since the zero-cable of a knot complement Y⊂XY\subset X is just the connected sum of XX with the unknot complement in S3S^{3}; the 1/q1/q-cable is just a change of framing; and the 1/01/0-cable, which changes the framing by zero, is the identity cable. We then have the following.

Theorem 5.4.

Suppose that p,q∈ℤp,q\in{\mathbb{Z}} with p>1p>1 and gcd⁡(p,q)=1\gcd(p,q)=1, and that Y=X∖ν⁡(K)Y=X\setminus\nu(K) is a boundary incompressible Floer simple knot complement in an L-space XX, with L-space interval ℒ⁡(Y)=[[a−b−,a+b+]]\mathcal{L}(Y)=[[\frac{a_{-}}{b_{-}},\frac{a_{+}}{b_{+}}]], written in terms of the surgery basis μ,λ∈H1​(∂Y)\mu,\lambda\in H_{1}(\partial Y) for KK, with μ\mu the meridian of KK and λ\lambda a choice of longitude. Then in terms of the surgery basis produced by cabling, the (p,q)(p,q)-cable Y(p,q)⊂XY^{(p,q)}\mkern-2.0mu\subset\mkern-2.0muX of Y⊂XY\mkern-2.0mu\subset\mkern-2.0muX has L-space interval

(113) ℒ⁡(Y(p,q))={{∞}a−b−∈[p∗q∗,∞],a+b+∈[q−p∗p−q∗,qp⟩∪{∞}[[1/y+,1/y−]]otherwise,\mathcal{L}(Y^{(p,q)})=\begin{cases}\{\infty\}&\mkern 15.0mu\mathord{\raise 0.49991pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.4pt}{}{a_-\mkern-2mu}{b_-\mkern-2mu}$}}\in\left[\mathord{\raise 0.49991pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.4pt}{}{p^*}{q^*}$}},\infty\right],\;\mathord{\raise 0.49991pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.4pt}{}{a_+\mkern-2mu}{b_+\mkern-2mu}$}}\in\left[\mathord{\raise 0.49991pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.4pt}{}{q-p^*}{p-q^*}$}},\mathord{\raise 0.49991pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.4pt}{}{q}{p}$}}\right>\cup\{\infty\}\\ [[1/y_{+},1/y_{-}]]&\mkern 15.0mu\text{otherwise},\end{cases}
