6. Observations

Our demonstration of extended L/NTF-equivalence for graph manifolds in Theorem 4.5 gives a (mildly) alternate proof of the Theorem 1.3 statement that a graph manifold is an L-space if and only if it fails to admit a co-oriented taut foliation.

From a practical standpoint, however, the main utility of Theorem 4.5 for us was its implication that the gluing result in Proposition 4.4 holds for all graph manifolds:

Corollary 6.1.

If Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} are non-solid-torus graph manifolds with torus boundary, then the union Y1∪φY2Y_{1}\mkern-1.0mu\cup_{\varphi}\!Y_{2}, with gluing map φ:∂Y1→−∂Y2\varphi\mkern-1.0mu:\mkern-1.0mu\partial Y_{1}\to-\partial Y_{2}, is an L-space if and only if

φ∗ℙ​(ℒ∘​(Y1))∪ℒ∘​(Y2)=ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y2)).\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{1}))\cup\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{2})={\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y_{2})).

Corollary 6.1 has two advantages over the more general L-space gluing criterion of Proposition  3.3: it removes the condition that φ∗ℙ​(ℒ∘​(Y1))∩ℒ∘​(Y2)\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{1}))\cap\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{2}) be nonempty, and it allows one to prove that Y1∪Y2Y_{1}\cup Y_{2} is not an L-space in cases in which boundary incompressible Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} are not Floer simple.

6.1. Generalization of Theorem 4.6

Nevertheless, while the L-space gluing result analogous to Proposition 3.3 proved by Hanselman and Watson in [19] replaces the hypothesis of Floer simplicity by a more technical condition, their gluing result does not impose the hypothesis of nonempty φ∗ℙ​(ℒ∘​(Y1))∩ℒ∘​(Y2)\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{1}))\cap\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{2}) required by the gluing result of J. Rasmussen and the author in [33]. In [18], the four authors discuss how these two gluing results can be combined to prove a gluing result analogous to Proposition 3.3 which requires Floer simplicity but not nonempty φ∗ℙ​(ℒ∘​(Y1))∩ℒ∘​(Y2)\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{1}))\cap\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{2}). Thus, the only real hypothesis we have circumvented is that of Floer simplicity. If we replace the condition that the YiY_{i} glued to M^\hat{M} be graph manifolds with the condition that they be Floer simple, then we can extend the domain of validity of Proposition 4.7 and Theorem 4.6 as follows.

Corollary 6.2.

Theorem  4.6 holds for any boundary incompressible Floer simple three-manifolds Y1,…,YngY_{1},\ldots,Y_{n_{{\textsc{g}}}}, provided that YY satisfies the criteria in Proposition 4.7 for ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) to be nonempty.

6.2. Generalized Solid Tori

A recent result of Gillespie [17] states that a compact oriented three-manifold YY with torus boundary satisfies ℒ⁡(Y)=ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y))∖{l}\mathcal{L}(Y)\mkern-1.5mu={\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y))\mkern-1.0mu\setminus\mkern-1.0mu\{l\} if and only if YY\! has genus 0 and an L-space filling. Such manifolds, called generalized solid tori in [33], are of independent interest.

In the proof of Theorem 4.6 and Proposition 4.7, we find many generalized solid tori with the regular fiber class as rational longitude, but there are limited circumstances in which other generalized solid tori appear. In fact, we can prove the following.

Theorem 6.3.

If YY\! is a graph manifold with torus boundary, b1​(Y)=1b_{1}(Y)\mkern-2.5mu=\mkern-2.5mu1, and rational longitude other than the regular fiber, then YY is a generalized solid torus if and only if it is homeomorphic to an iterated cable of the regular fiber complement in S1×S2S^{1}\mkern-2.5mu\times\mkern-0.8muS^{2}\mkern-4.0mu.

Proof.

Suppose YY is a generalized solid torus graph manifold, with rational longitude ll not coinciding with the regular fiber. Since YY is Floer simple with ∞∈ℒ∘​(Y)\infty\in\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y), YY must satisfy (fs3)(\textsc{fs3}\mkern-0.5mu) from Proposition 4.7, and since y−,y+≠∞y_{-},y_{+}\mkern-2.0mu\neq\mkern-2.0mu\infty, we must have ∞≠yi−g≥yi+g≠∞\infty\neq y_{i-}^{\textsc{g}}\geq y_{i+}^{\textsc{g}}\neq\infty. Claim 2 from Section 4.7 then implies y−>y+y_{-}\mkern-3.5mu>\mkern-2.0muy_{+} unless ng=1n_{{\textsc{g}}}\mkern-4.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu1 with nd≤1n_{{\textsc{d}}}\mkern-3.0mu\leq\mkern-2.0mu1 or ng=0n_{{\textsc{g}}}\mkern-4.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu0 with nd≤2n_{{\textsc{d}}}\mkern-3.0mu\leq\mkern-2.0mu2.

If ng=1n_{{\textsc{g}}}\mkern-2.0mu=\mkern-2.0mu1, then according to Claim 4 from Section 4.8, either y1d∈ℤy_{1}^{\textsc{d}}\in{\mathbb{Z}}, in which case YY is homeomorphic to Y1Y_{1} and we should replace YY with Y1Y_{1} and begin again; or y−1g=y+1g=:y1gy_{-1}^{\textsc{g}}=y_{+1}^{\textsc{g}}=:y_{1}^{\textsc{g}} with y1d+y1g∈ℤy_{1}^{\textsc{d}}+y_{1}^{\textsc{g}}\in{\mathbb{Z}}, in which case Y1Y_{1} is a generalized solid torus, and Proposition 5.1 implies Y⊂Y⁡(l)Y\subset Y(l) is a cable of Y1⊂Y1​(l)Y_{1}\subset Y_{1}(l).

If ng=0n_{{\textsc{g}}}=0, then YY is Seifert fibered with y−=y+y_{-}=y_{+}, and so either from [33] or from a mildly modified version of Claim 4, we deduce that either y1d+y2d∈ℤy_{1}^{\textsc{d}}+y_{2}^{\textsc{d}}\in\mathbb{Z}, in which case Proposition 5.1 implies YY\! is a cable of the regular fiber complement in S1×S2S^{1}\mkern-4.0mu\times\!S^{2}; or {y1d,y2d}∩ℤ≠∅\{y_{1}^{\textsc{d}},y_{2}^{\textsc{d}}\}\mkern-1.0mu\cap\mkern-1.0mu{\mathbb{Z}}\mkern-2.0mu\neq\mkern-2.0mu\emptyset, in which case Y\mkern-1.0muY\mkern-2.5mu is a solid torus, hence homeomorphic to the regular fiber complement in S1×S2S^{1}\mkern-3.5mu\times\mkern-2.5muS^{2}\!\!.

The converse is an immediate corollary of Proposition 5.1 and Theorem 4.6. ∎

We also have the following result for arbitrary generalized solid tori.

Proposition 6.4.

If YY is a generalized solid torus, then any cable of Y⊂Y⁡(l)Y\subset Y(l) is a generalized solid torus.

Proof.

If YY is boundary compressible, then it is the connected sum of a solid torus with lens spaces, and Theorem 6.3 implies that any cable of a solid torus within its longitudinal filling is a generalized solid torus. If YY is boundary incompressible, then the result is an immediate corollary of Theorem 5.2. ∎

Similarly, for any class of manifolds for which the gluing result in Proposition 1.5 holds without the requirement of Floer simplicity—such as graph manifolds—one has the result that if YY has an isolated L-space filling, i.e., if ℒ⁡(Y)={μ}\mathcal{L}(Y)=\{\mu\} for some μ∈ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y))\mu\in{\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)), then any cable of Y⊂Y⁡(μ)Y\subset Y(\mu) has Y⁡(μ)Y(\mu) as an isolated L-space filling.

6.3. Isolated L-space fillings

A Seifert fiber complement in an L-space Seifert fibered manifold could justifiably be called the prototypical Floer simple manifold, just as a lens space is the prototypical L-space. It is therefore striking that we encounter isolated L-space fillings as regular fiber complements in graph manifolds. Fortunately, this still does not prevent L-space graph manifolds from admitting Floer simple Seifert fiber complements.

Given a closed graph manifold XX, we shall call an exceptional fiber fe⊂Xf_{\textsc{e}}\subset X invariantly exceptional if the JSJ componenent Y^⊂X\hat{Y}\subset X containing fef_{\textsc{e}} has more than one exceptional fiber. To motivate this name, note that if XX has more than one JSJ component and Y^\hat{Y} has only one exceptional fiber, say, of slope y1d=y0y_{1}^{\textsc{d}}=y_{0}, then since the punctured solid torus has nonunique Seifert structure, XX is homemorphic to a graph manifold in which y1dy_{1}^{\textsc{d}} is replaced with 00 and φ1∗ℙ\varphi_{1*}^{{\mathbb{P}}} is replaced with φ1∗ℙ+y0\varphi_{1*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}\!+y_{0}.

Theorem 6.5.

Every invariantly exceptional fiber complement in an L-space graph manifold is Floer simple.

Proof.

Suppose XX is an L-space graph manifold. If XX is Seifert fibered, then every Seifert fiber complement, regular or otherwise, is Floer simple.

Suppose XX has more than one JSJ component, and let YY denote a non-Floer-simple complement of an invariantly exceptional fiber. Since ℒ⁡(Y)≠∅\mathcal{L}(Y)\neq\emptyset, YY non-Floer-simple implies ℒ⁡(Y)={y−}={y+}\mathcal{L}(Y)=\{y_{-}\}=\{y_{+}\}, with y±∈ℚy_{\pm}\in{\mathbb{Q}}. However, since YY has at least one exceptional fiber, Proposition 4.14 tells us that y−=y+∈ℤy_{-}=y_{+}\in{\mathbb{Z}}, contradicting the hypothesis that YY is an exceptional fiber complement of XX. Thus the theorem holds. ∎

On the other hand, for a graph manifold with more than one JSJ component, Seifert fibers are not the only knots yielding Floer simple knot complements, due to the following result for arbitrary L-spaces.

Proposition 6.6.

If an L-space XX decomposes as a union Y1∪φY2Y_{1}\cup_{\varphi}\!Y_{2} of Floer simple manifolds YiY_{i} along an incompressible torus T⊂XT\subset X, then there is a knot K⊂XK\subset X transversely intersecting TT for which knot the complement X∖ν⁡(K)X\setminus\nu(K) is Floer simple.

Proof.

In fact, an analogous result holds for any toroidal L-space.

Suppose the above hypotheses hold. Then since Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} are Floer simple with incompressible boundary, Proposition 3.3 implies

(119) φ∗ℙ​(ℒ∘​(Y1))∪ℒ∘​(Y2)=ℙ⁡(H1​(∂Y2)).\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{1}))\cup\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{2})={\mathbb{P}}(H_{1}(\partial Y_{2})).

Since φ∗ℙ​(ℒ∘​(Y1))\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{1})) and ℒ∘​(Y2)\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{2}) are open, (119) implies they intersect. Choosing any μ2∈φ∗ℙ​(ℒ∘​(Y1))∩ℒ∘​(Y2)\mu_{2}\in\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{1}))\cap\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{2}), set μ1:=φ∗ℙ−1​(μ2)\mu_{1}:=\varphi_{*}^{{\mathbb{P}}\mkern 1.0mu-1}(\mu_{2}), and let KiK_{i} denote the knot core of Yi​(μi)∖YiY_{i}(\mu_{i})\setminus Y_{i}. As explained in more detail in the proof of [33, Theorem 6.2], XX can be regarded as zero-surgery on the knot K1​#​K2⊂Y1​(μ1)​#​Y2​(μ2)K_{1}\#K_{2}\subset Y_{1}(\mu_{1})\#Y_{2}(\mu_{2}). Thus, if we set Y:=Y1​(μ1)​#​Y2​(μ2)∖ν⁡(K1​#​K2)Y:=Y_{1}(\mu_{1})\#Y_{2}(\mu_{2})\setminus\nu(K_{1}\#K_{2}) and let KK denote the knot core of X∖YX\setminus Y, then the knot complement Y=X∖ν⁡(K)Y=X\setminus\nu(K) has at least two distinct L-space fillings, hence is Floer simple. Moreover, since KK is dual to K1​#​K2K_{1}\#K_{2} under surgery, KK intersects the separating torus transversely. ∎

Corollary 6.7.

If XX is an L-space graph manifold, then for every incompressible torus T⊂XT\subset X, there is a knot K⊂XK\subset X transversely intersecting TT for which knot the complement X∖ν⁡(K)X\setminus\nu(K) is Floer simple.

Proof.

Choose an arbitrary incompressible torus T⊂XT\subset X, not necessarily one used in the minimal JSJ decomposition for XX, and write X=Y1∪TY2X=Y_{1}\cup_{T}Y_{2}. Since XX is an L-space, Corollary 6.1 implies each YiY_{i} has nonempty ℒ∘​(Yi)\mathcal{L}^{\circ}(Y_{i}), hence is Floer simple. Thus, we can apply Proposition 6.6. ∎

This section has only cataloged the most obvious corollaries of the paper’s main results. We invite the reader to find more.
